The desk files the mechanism as verified, the incentive as verified, and the million-scale count as claimed-but-unproven, in the ledger below—the same column, the reader will note, as the largest claims of the other side.

6. The Comparative Ledger: Windows Are the World Norm

Every state on the desk’s shelf grants the visitor a window and attaches consequences to outstaying it; the United States is unexceptional in kind and specific only in its numbers. The Schengen area—twenty-nine European states, including non-EU members Switzerland (a member since 2008), Norway, and Iceland—admits the visa-exempt short-stay visitor for ninety days in any 180-day period, and the clock is cumulative: it is a rolling window counted backward from each day of presence, so a departure does not reset it, and the traveler who has spent ninety days inside must spend ninety outside before the arithmetic admits him again; the popular border-hop reading of the rule is a misreading, and the strategy sometimes built on it—sitting out the clock in a nearby non-member state—works only where the waiting state is genuinely outside the area, as the United Kingdom and Ireland are, and fails where it is not, as Switzerland is not outside it. Overstay consequences inside the area include fines, recorded alerts, and entry bans that vary by state from months to years. Canada admits the ordinary visitor for up to six months as stamped or presumed at entry, extendable on application. Common grants elsewhere run thirty days (much of Southeast Asia’s visa-exempt practice), ninety days (Japan, Brazil, and the Schengen norm), and six months (the United Kingdom’s standard visitor, Canada, and the United States’ own B-2). Where clocks are per-entry rather than cumulative—in the thirty-day regimes—the visa run is a real institution, with its border towns and same-day return buses, and states that tire of it convert to cumulative counting or per-year caps, which is the direction of travel in the systems the desk examined. The structure is everywhere the same three parts: a window, an accounting, and a price for exceeding both.

Germany’s file is the desk’s exhibit of the accounting run as routine administration. A person who takes up residence registers the address with the municipal office—the Anmeldung, due within fourteen days of moving in, producing the registration certificate on which the rest of German administrative life depends: bank account, tax class, health insurance, the residence file itself. The non-European who stays beyond the Schengen short-stay window holds a residence permit, the Aufenthaltserlaubnis, issued for a stated purpose—work, study, family—by the local foreigners’ authority, time-limited, renewable on the purpose continuing, and ripening toward a settlement permit on years, language, and contributions. Nothing in the arrangement is ceremonial: it is a ledger of who is present, on what basis, until when, kept by clerks, and its premise—that presence in the territory is an accounted condition rather than a default—is the premise of every system in this section, including the American one. The desk files the comparison without a moral: the states differ in window length, in ripening rules, and in the price of the overage, and they do not differ in keeping the ledger.

7. The Overstay Category: The Larger Half of the Flow

The Department of Homeland Security counts the overstay every year, and the count is the largest single exhibit in this report. The Entry/Exit Overstay Report for fiscal 2024 records 46,657,108 expected departures of nonimmigrant visitors arriving by air and sea, and 538,548 overstay events—a total overstay rate of 1.15 percent—of which 482,954 were suspected in-country overstays at the report’s close, a figure that had fallen to 427,204 by February 2025 as late departures and status adjustments resolved. The largest national counts are Mexico (61,442), Colombia (28,409), India (27,585), and Canada (25,309, at a rate of only 0.27 percent of Canadian departures); the visa-waiver states’ suspected in-country rate is 0.43 percent, the non-waiver rate excluding Canada and Mexico 2.22 percent, and the student and exchange categories (F, M, J) run at 2.45 percent, while the highest rates belong to small programs—Myanmar at 43 percent, Suriname at 31, Haiti at 25—where a few thousand admissions produce the percentage. The category’s weight is in the accumulation: the Center for Migration Studies has estimated, in a series of studies running back a decade, that overstays have exceeded entries without inspection among new additions to the unauthorized population in every year since about 2007, reaching roughly three-fifths of new additions in peak years and about 40 percent of the newly unauthorized in fiscal 2023—which is to say, the characteristic modern entrant into unlawful status is a person who arrived inspected, with a visa, and stayed past the date on the I-94. The stock figures bound the flow: the Pew Research Center’s estimate puts the unauthorized population at about 14 million in 2023, a record, against about 11 million in the department’s own earlier series—estimates, both, built from census residuals, and filed as estimates wherever this report repeats them.

8. Exposure Over Time: The Resident’s Ledger of Tripwires

Consider the resident the system actually holds: admitted lawfully, employed for decades, remitting wages, raising citizen children—and carrying, for every day of those decades, the full deportability list of section 3. His exposure is not a mood but an inventory, and the desk files the inventory as he accumulates it. The moral-turpitude rules run on two clocks: one CIMT committed within five years of admission, on a charge carrying a possible year’s sentence, is a ground; two CIMTs not from a single scheme are a ground at any time. The aggravated-felony definition runs on sentence arithmetic: a theft or burglary plea with one year imposed—suspended in full, served not a day—is inside it, as is a fraud with $10,001 of loss and a drug offense that the charging statute calls trafficking at quantities the street calls personal. The controlled-substance ground admits one exception and one only, the single thirty-gram marijuana possession case. The domestic-violence ground, §237(a)(2)(E), reaches crimes against a protected person and violations of protection orders, and its definitions are litigated household by household. The false-claim ground—a claim to citizenship made for a purpose or benefit, on a driver’s license form or an I-9 as readily as at a naturalization interview—carries, on the inadmissibility side, a bar with no general waiver, relieved only by a narrow exception for the child of citizens who reasonably believed the claim. Unlawful voting is its own ground on both lists. Alien smuggling includes driving a relative across or paying his guide, subject to a discretionary family waiver on one list and not the other. The address-registration ground is rarely charged and entirely on the books. Abandonment can be found in the pattern of his trips home. And overlaying the whole inventory, the disposition of his case if charged depends on relief whose elements—good moral character above all—are themselves forfeited by entries in the same inventory. No single line is exotic; the exposure is the sum, carried without expiry.

The bar fight is the cleanest test of the inventory, and the desk runs it as the record runs it: the same night ends in three different countries of outcome depending on the charge, the plea, and the sentence. Simple assault—an ordinary fight, no weapon, no serious injury—is generally not a crime involving moral turpitude, because the offense requires no intent to steal, defraud, or commit an inherently base act; the immigration courts have found turpitude where the statute adds an aggravator: a weapon, intent to injure seriously, a protected victim. It is likewise not an aggravated felony as a “crime of violence” unless the offense is a felony under the elements clause of 18 U.S.C. §16 as preserved by Dimaya and the term of imprisonment imposed is at least one year—imposed, again, not served, the suspended year counting in full. The hinges are therefore clerical: whether the prosecutor charges the simple or the aggravated form; whether the plea is taken to assault, to disorderly conduct, to a theft count offered in substitution; whether the sentence negotiated is 364 days or 365—a distinction with no meaning in the criminal court’s own purposes and the whole meaning in the immigration court’s. A resident of forty years who pleads to a misdemeanor assault with a 364-day suspended sentence has ordinarily bought a criminal record and kept his residence; the same man, pleading to the same conduct on a differently drawn statute with a year imposed, has purchased an aggravated felony, mandatory detention, ineligibility for nearly all relief, and removal under the administrative track without a merits hearing on his equities. Between those two outcomes stands no finding about the man. There stands a charging document and a sentencing line.

Most of those documents are written in plea negotiations, and until 2010 the immigration consequences were not required to be in the room. In Padilla v. Kentucky, 559 U.S. 356 (2010), the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment requires defense counsel to advise a noncitizen client when a plea carries a risk of deportation—precisely and personally where the statute makes the consequence clear, in general terms where it is not—because deportation is, in the Court’s words, a particularly severe penalty intimately related to the criminal process. Chaidez v. United States, 568 U.S. 342 (2013), confined the rule to cases after 2010, leaving the earlier decades’ pleas where they lie. The working system the two decisions describe is this: the criminal courts dispose of the overwhelming majority of their cases by plea; the plea’s immigration weight is fixed by category-matching between the statute of conviction and the federal lists, an exercise neither the prosecutor’s offer sheet nor the defendant’s intuition performs unaided; and the immigration-safe plea—the substituted count, the 364-day sentence—is a known technology, available where counsel on both sides know to ask for it and invisible where they do not. A large share of the conviction-based removals in section 4’s series were manufactured in that room, on charges whose immigration valence nobody at the table had priced. The desk files this not as an indictment of the plea system but as its operating description, supplied by the Supreme Court itself.

The time dimension completes the exposure: deportability has no statute of limitations. A conviction entered in the third year of a residence may be charged in the thirty-seventh, when it surfaces—in a naturalization fingerprint check, a travel screening, a later arrest’s booking referral—and the government’s delay is no defense in the proceeding. Lawful permanent residence does not ripen: there is no term of years after which the §237 list ceases to apply to the resident, no doctrine of repose in the deportability statute, and the resident’s protection is therefore never his longevity but only the absence of a chargeable event and the presence, if charged, of a relief whose character elements his record still satisfies. Exactly one event ends the exposure, and it is the subject of section 10: naturalization, after which the former resident is a citizen, removable no longer, and answerable to the immigration law only through the narrow door of denaturalization for fraud in the procurement itself. The exposure ledger and the definitions ledger are the same ledger read at two ends: between admission and oath, the resident carries the list; the oath is the only discharge the book provides.

9. Virtue Is Not a Defense: What the Statute Asks and What It Does Not

The grounds of removability in INA §237 contain no character credit. Read as a list—and section 3 above is the list—the grounds are categories of status and conduct: admitted or not, registered or not, convicted or not, of enumerated offenses, within enumerated periods. No subsection asks whether the respondent is industrious, charitable, devout, beloved, or the support of a household; no defense in the proceeding consists of being good. The statute’s character inquiry exists, but it is stationed elsewhere, and the placement is the point: “good moral character” is an element of benefits and relief—a condition of naturalization under §316(a), of cancellation of removal under §240A(b)(1), of post-conclusion voluntary departure under §240B(b)—where it operates as a gate the applicant must pass, defined in part by a disqualifier list at §101(f) that includes habitual drunkenness, certain convictions, and false testimony. Character, in the statute’s architecture, can qualify a person for mercy or for membership; it cannot excuse a status violation, because the violation is not charged as a failure of character. The removable saint and the removable felon stand in the same posture before §237, differentiated only by the relief each can reach—and the desk notes, as a matter of the same record, that the relief map is itself drawn in conduct: the felon’s aggravated felony closes doors the saint’s clean record leaves open. The system is not indifferent to virtue out of absent-mindedness. It is built so that virtue is currency in the relief market and legal tender nowhere else.

The case the argument reaches for is, in the record, a case about channels. The hypothetical posed in the public debate is of a figure of universal charitable reputation—the record’s standing example is Mother Teresa of Calcutta, Albanian-born, a citizen of India, founder of the Missionaries of Charity—entering the United States to do religious work without status: on the statute as written, she would be removable, because the grounds in section 3 would apply to her as to anyone, and her works would appear in her case only as equities in a discretionary request. The record adds what the hypothetical omits. A dedicated lawful channel exists for exactly her case and has for generations: the R-1 nonimmigrant classification at §101(a)(15)(R) admits religious workers—ministers and persons in religious vocations, members of a denomination with a bona fide nonprofit religious organization in the United States, coming to work for it—for up to five years, and the EB-4 special-immigrant category admits religious workers to permanent residence. And the historical case itself ran through the law’s front door and past it: by Public Law 104-218, enacted October 1, 1996, Congress conferred honorary citizenship of the United States on her, making her one of eight persons so honored in the republic’s history and one of two—with Winston Churchill, in 1963—honored in her lifetime. The State Department’s own manual (8 FAM 306.1) records the honor’s legal content: honorary citizenship confers no special entry, travel, or immigration benefits, and its holder is not eligible for a United States passport. Which is to say, the republic’s highest civic compliment left its recipient’s immigration position exactly where the statute put it, and the honor and the removability coexisted in the same file without contradiction, because they answer different questions. The desk files the exhibit at that temperature: the statute is virtue-blind; the channels exist; the actual case used them.

10. “Naturalization”: A Definitions Section

The word does one job in the statute and another in the argument, and the desk files both. In law, naturalization is the defined process by which a person not born a citizen becomes one, at INA §§310–347 (8 U.S.C. §§1421–1459). Its core requirements stand at §316(a): the applicant must be a lawful permanent resident for five years (three, under §319(a), if married to and living with a citizen); must show continuous residence and physical presence for at least half that period; must show good moral character for the statutory period against the §101(f) disqualifiers; must demonstrate English proficiency and knowledge of United States history and government under §312, subject to age, disability, and long-residence exceptions; must show attachment to the principles of the Constitution; and must take the oath of allegiance at §337, renouncing prior allegiances. Citizenship so acquired is near-absolute against the state: it can be undone only by denaturalization in federal court under §340, for illegal procurement or material concealment in the process itself—a door the government has used sparingly and the courts supervise closely. Beside the statutory word stands the colloquial one, in which long residence is said to “naturalize” a person into a place—to make him, in substance, of it—with entitlement argued to follow from the substance. United States law contains no such ripening for the non-resident, and it contains exactly one fossil of the idea: the registry provision, §249, which permits a person of good moral character present since a fixed date to register into residence—a date Congress set at June 28, 1940 in 1929, advanced by stages to June 30, 1948, and last advanced by the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 to January 1, 1972, where it has remained for forty years, a door built for a generation that has now passed through it or died. Residence ripens into status by rule in other systems on the shelf—the European Union’s long-term resident status attaches after five years of legal residence under Council Directive 2003/109/EC—and the desk files the contrast as it files the others: a design choice, present there, absent here, its presence or absence a fact about statutes and not about the worth of the residents.

Acquisition at birth, the other door, runs on two principles whose distribution is itself a ledger. Jus soli—citizenship by birth on the territory—is the rule of the United States under the Fourteenth Amendment and INA §301(a) (“born in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof”), and of most of the Americas, Canada and nearly all of Latin America included. Jus sanguinis—citizenship by descent—is the rule of most of Europe and Asia, transmitted through a citizen parent wherever the birth occurs; the United States applies it abroad at §301(c)–(g) beside its soil rule. Pure forms are now rare: Germany, the historic sanguinis case, added a soil element in 2000 for children of long-resident foreigners; Ireland restricted its soil rule by referendum in 2004, the last European state to retire an unconditional one; France mixes both with residence-based acquisition at majority; Israel’s Law of Return is a descent-and-identity rule of its own kind. The desk’s observation is bookkeeping: every state on earth assigns membership at birth by some combination of soil and blood and then administers a defined door—naturalization—for everyone else, and the definitions, not the affections of the public, are what the doors are made of. What the colloquial usage asks for is that the door be deemed walked through by time served. No statute on the shelf deems it; some legislatures have built versions of it; the American registry stands in the book as the record that the idea was enacted once, dated, and not renewed.

11. The Public Vocabulary: Two Phrases and a Frame, Examined

The desk applies its definitions instrument to the phrases the argument is conducted in, beginning with the enforcement side’s. “Bad hombres” entered the record in the third presidential debate of October 19, 2016, at Las Vegas, in the Republican nominee’s answer on immigration: “One of my first acts will be to get all of the drug lords, all of the bad ones—we have some bad, bad people in this country that have to go out. We’re going to get them out; we’re going to secure the border. And once the border is secured, at a later date, we’ll make a determination as to the rest. But we have some bad hombres here, and we’re going to get them out.” Grammatically the phrase names a class—in context, the drug lords and the “bad ones”—and the sentence around it makes a testable promise with two parts: enforcement’s first acts would fall on the criminal class, and the disposition of “the rest” would be determined later. The desk tests the promise against the record it has already filed, in section 4’s series, and states the fit plainly: in every year in the series, including the years of explicit priority enforcement before the phrase was coined and the years after, the convicted were a majority of interior removals—82 percent in fiscal 2013, 91 percent in 2015, 93 percent criminal-involved in 2024—and a minority of removals overall wherever the border fast tracks supplied the volume, falling to 32.7 percent conviction-or-charge in fiscal 2024 and lower in 2025, because the majority of the removed in the modern system are processed where they are caught, at the border, a population selected by geography rather than by record. The phrase’s class exists in the data; it has never described the whole of the removed, and in the most recent years it describes the smallest share of them since ICE began publishing the split. Whether that arithmetic honors or betrays the promise of October 2016 is an argument the desk leaves to its makers; the instrument’s reading is that the promise was kept in the interior, where it could be targeted, and swamped in the total, where it could not.

The opposition’s phrase is of a different grammatical species, and the desk files it as what it is: a claim about legitimacy, not about law. “No one is illegal on stolen land”—of uncertain coinage, in mass circulation on signs and murals by the late 2010s—asserts that the enforcing sovereign holds its territory by conquest, and that a title so acquired cannot make presence wrongful. As logic, the premise addresses the legitimacy of the United States’ jurisdiction, not the content of the Immigration and Nationality Act; nothing in the sentence engages §212 or §237, and it would stand or fall identically if both were repealed tomorrow and replaced. As law, it is not cognizable in the forum where removals are decided: an immigration judge’s jurisdiction runs to the statute and the regulations, challenges to the court’s authority over the respondent are resolved against the challenger as a matter of course, and the doctrinal ground was settled a century before the phrase—the federal power over admission and removal is an incident of sovereignty, in the line of cases from the Chinese Exclusion Case, 130 U.S. 581 (1889), through Fong Yue Ting v. United States, 149 U.S. 698 (1893), which held removal to be not punishment but the withdrawal of a privilege of residence, a holding never overruled. The forums in which the premise could be acted on are the legislative and constitutional ones—a Congress persuaded by it could repeal the bars, a constitutional amendment could restructure the power—which is to say the phrase is a political argument wearing a legal sentence’s clothes, and graded as politics it competes with other politics. The desk adds its one filed observation, as comparative record rather than rebuttal: the premise, taken at full strength, runs against every state on earth, since every administering state on the shelf—Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Mexico, and the European states included—governs entry on land acquired by conquest at some depth in its history, and each of them keeps a removals ledger of the kind filed in section 6. A principle that invalidates all of them equally distinguishes none of them, and the desk files it, at that grade, in the ledger.

The third specimen is not a phrase but the frame both phrases share, and it is the frame the statute answers. The deservingness frame holds that removal is a judgment on the person—that the good should be unremovable because good, and, in its mirror form, that the removed are by the fact of removal shown bad. The record in this report answers the frame, rather than either of its users: the removability grounds ask nothing about desert (section 9); the criminal series shows the removed to be, in the majority of recent years, persons with no conviction at all (section 4); and the exposure ledger shows the resident’s safety to rest on clerical hinges—a charging decision, a sentence line—rather than on any ledger of his deserts (section 8). The desk files the frame as the debate’s central misdescription of the machinery, in both its directions, and proceeds to the scale of the machine itself.

12. Scale: The System in Numbers

The machine’s dimensions, filed with their years and their counters, because the counters disagree in instructive ways. Removals. Counting ICE’s removals only: 142,580 in fiscal 2023; 271,484 in fiscal 2024; about 320,000 in fiscal 2025 by USAFacts’ compilation, 329,018 by the independent reconstruction from ICE’s biweekly releases; and 356,389 in fiscal 2026 through July 11, 2026, by ICE’s figures as reported—against a department-wide DHS removal count of 183,360 for fiscal 2023 and 329,990 for fiscal 2024 in the Office of Homeland Security Statistics’ series, which folds in CBP-executed removals, and a modern single-year record of 438,421 total removals set in fiscal 2013. The two families of numbers measure different machines—one agency’s execution docket against the department’s whole ledger—and any public figure for “deportations” that does not name its counter is filed by this desk as incomplete on its face. The courts. TRAC’s case-level count puts the immigration-court backlog at 3,037,800 pending cases at the end of September 2026, of whom 2,259,317 have filed asylum applications; EOIR’s aggregate tables print higher figures—3,722,776 at the end of fiscal 2025, 3,469,569 at fiscal 2026’s third quarter—the two series counting cases and files by different rules; the Justice Department recorded a decline of more than 447,000 from January 2025 to September 2025 against its own earlier peak above 4.18 million, while immigration judges issued 485,456 removal orders in fiscal 2025, up 57 percent on the year, 306,557 of them in absentia, by the Congressional Research Service’s figures. The court that carries this sits 557 judges, down from 735 at the fiscal 2024 peak. The dockets. ICE’s non-detained docket: above 7.6 million at the end of fiscal 2024; 7.3 million in February 2026 (CRS), carrying an estimated 1.6 million final orders, up from 1,445,549 counted in November 2024. Detention. On July 11, 2026, by TRAC’s tabulation of ICE data, 65,765 people were in ICE detention, of whom 70.6 percent—46,436—had no criminal conviction and 39.8 percent had neither a conviction nor a pending charge; the alternatives-to-detention population stood at 183,181; the detained count had touched roughly 73,000 at its late-2025 peak, a record, against funded capacity built for a fraction of it. The staff. ERO’s deportation officers numbered about 6,100 before 2025; the July 2025 reconciliation act carried $75 billion for ICE, including funding to hire 10,000; federal personnel data put the agency’s total workforce at about 20,000 in December 2025 and 29,000 in July 2026, with nearly 12,000 hired between January 2025 and June 2026, the agency announcing in January 2026 that its officer and agent ranks had grown from 10,000 to 22,000—and more than 2,900 employees departing in the first half of 2026, the highest half-year attrition in the agency’s records. The desk files the growth and the churn in the same line, as the personnel data files them.

13. The Error File: Citizens, Wrongful Removals, and the Critics’ Claims on the Same Instrument

The critics’ central factual claim—that the machine removes people it has no authority to remove, including citizens—is documented by the government’s own auditors, at a scale those auditors themselves bound. The Government Accountability Office’s report GAO-21-487 (July 2021), examining fiscal 2015 through the second quarter of fiscal 2020, found that ICE had arrested 674, detained 121, and removed 70 individuals across the period whom its records identified as potential United States citizens; that detainers had been issued against at least 895 potential citizens, about 74 percent of them cancelled before action; and that ICE’s data on citizenship claims were too inconsistently recorded for the counts to be treated as more than floors. TRAC’s separate examination of the longer record counted at least 2,840 people wrongly flagged as removable between 2002 and 2017. Citizenship in these cases typically turns on derived and acquired citizenship through parents—the most documentarily tangled corner of the statute book—and the desk files the auditors’ own caveat with their counts: the record system that produces the removals does not reliably record the claims that would impeach them, so the true figure is unknowable from the published instruments, bounded below by the audits and asserted above them by advocates without an instrument of their own. The claim of wrongful removal of citizens is therefore filed as documented-but-small, with its denominator problem stated, and the claim of its nonexistence is filed, against the GAO, as disproven.

The single most litigated error of the current period is a matter of court record, and the desk files the record. In October 2019 an immigration judge granted Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who had entered without inspection in 2011, withholding of removal to El Salvador on a finding of likely persecution there, while leaving a removal order in place as to other countries. On March 15, 2025, he was removed to El Salvador and confined in its CECOT prison. In litigation filed by his family (Abrego Garcia v. Noem, No. 8:25-cv-00951, D. Md.), the acting ICE field office director declared under oath on March 31, 2025, that “[t]hrough administrative error, Abrego-Garcia was removed from the United States to El Salvador,” the removal having been carried out “in good faith based on the existence of a final order of removal” and the withholding grant overlooked. The district court ordered the government to facilitate and effectuate his return; the Supreme Court, on April 10, 2025, required the government to facilitate his release from custody in El Salvador. He was returned to the United States on June 6, 2025—into federal criminal custody, under a Tennessee indictment charging human smuggling, to which he has pleaded not guilty and against which a motion to dismiss for vindictive and selective prosecution is pending; the civil and criminal litigation continue at filing. The desk files the case for the machinery it exhibits and for nothing else: a subsisting court order was not executed by the system that held it, the error was conceded in the government’s own declaration, the judiciary’s corrective process ran for twelve weeks across two court systems and an international negotiation, and its resolution arrived fused with a prosecution. Claims that the case proves the system lawless, and claims that it proves the system self-correcting, are both filed as interpretations; the instrument records the sequence. Beside it, one line of the broader ledger: deaths in ICE custody reached 38 in fiscal 2026 on the agency’s published detainee-death reports, the highest annual count in its series—a figure each side cites for its own frame and which the desk files, with its source, as a count.

14. The Ledger

The whole subject, sorted by the state of its evidence. The desk closes the file with the four-column accounting the report has applied throughout, to the commissioner’s claims and to the opposition’s at the same grade. Verified: established by statute, official record, or adjudication. Documented-but-small: real, proven, and measured against a baseline that bounds its size. Claimed-but-unproven: asserted by named makers, with no instrument at the scale claimed. Disproven: tested by the instrument built to test it and failed.

VerifiedDocumented-but-smallClaimed-but-unprovenDisproven
Unlawful presence is a civil violation, not a crime (Arizona v. United States); improper entry and reentry after removal are crimes (8 U.S.C. §§1325–1326). The ladder runs NTA, hearings, BIA, final order, with expedited, administrative, and reinstatement tracks beside it. A removal order carries 5/10/20-year and permanent bars (§212(a)(9)(A)); voluntary departure carries no removal-order bar. Overstays have exceeded border entries among new unauthorized residents since about 2007 (CMS); 538,548 overstay events were counted in fiscal 2024 (DHS). The Schengen clock is cumulative, 90 in 180, and Switzerland is inside it. The removability grounds contain no character credit; good moral character gates benefits and relief only. A single ordinary DUI is not a deportability ground (Leocal; Lopez-Meza). Deportability has no statute of limitations; only naturalization ends a resident’s exposure. ICE removed 271,484 people in fiscal 2024, 32.7 percent with convictions or pending charges; the interior cut ran 93 percent criminal-involved. Europeans are removed—1,540 in fiscal 2023—under the same statute as everyone else. Wrongful arrests, detentions, and removals of potential citizens: 674 arrested, 121 detained, 70 removed, fiscal 2015–2020, by the GAO’s audit, whose own caveats make the counts floors. European removals: 1,540 of 183,360 formal removals in fiscal 2023, under 1 percent, against about 61,000 European visa-waiver overstays in fiscal 2024. The Abrego Garcia removal: one case, fully documented, error conceded by the agency in court. Deaths in ICE custody: 38 in fiscal 2026, the highest year in the agency’s series, against tens of thousands detained on any given day. Documented voluntary departures: 6,118 court grants in the first six months of 2025—a real channel, at documented scale. DHS’s count of 1.6–1.9 million “self-deportations” in 2025: built on survey population estimates, with no published methodology or departure count beneath it. The claim of a million-scale population of unlawfully present Ukrainians and Eastern Europeans: no DHS table at scale supports it; the measured European overstay stock is real and smaller, and most post-2022 Ukrainians hold parole or TPS. The “80 percent” non-criminal share as a constant of the system: no official series states it; the measured series runs 41 percent non-convicted (fiscal 2013) to roughly two-thirds (fiscal 2024) and higher in 2025. The department’s 622,000-deportations claim for 2025 as a figure comparable to the ICE removal series. That elections—or removals—are administered on any basis other than the statutory one, asserted without an instrument: no specimen at scale has been produced in this file, from any direction. That a single DUI forfeits a green card under current law: Leocal and Lopez-Meza dispose of it; the bill that would make it so, H.R. 875, passed the House in June 2025 and is not law. That criminals are put in deportation facilities instead of jail: the detainer record shows criminal custody and sentence first, ICE custody after. That the border hop resets the Schengen clock: the 90/180 rule is a rolling cumulative window. That “bad hombres” describes the removed population as a whole: the convicted have been a minority of total removals in every recent year of ICE’s published split. That wrongful removal of citizens does not occur: the GAO’s audit is the disposing instrument. That long residence alone ripens into lawful status in the United States: the registry door stands frozen at January 1, 1972, and no other provision enacts the ripening.

As the file stands on Sunday, November 8, 2026: deportation in the United States is an administrative process built on two statute lists—inadmissibility for those at the door, deportability for those admitted—run through a court track with hearings and appeals and three faster tracks without them, ending in bars of five, ten, and twenty years for the removed, no removal bar for the voluntarily departed, and unlawful-presence bars that turn on time accrued however a person leaves; its recent caseload is majority non-criminal in the totals and majority criminal in the interior, its overstay flow has exceeded its border flow among new arrivals for nearly two decades, its court backlog stands above three million cases, its final orders outstanding above 1.4 million, its detention population near record levels with seven in ten detainees holding no conviction, and its statute asks nothing, at the removability stage, about whether the person before it is good; the resident it holds longest is exposed for the whole of his residence to a list of tripwires that never expire until the oath of naturalization discharges them; the government’s own auditors have documented its errors against citizens at small, real scale; and every large claim in the public argument—the millions self-deported, the eighty percent, the criminal flood, the spotless machine—grades, on the instruments available, below the arithmetic the record actually keeps. The log proceeds.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Twenty items.

Subjective
Immigration and Nationality Act — 8 U.S.C. §§1101, 1182, 1227, 1427 (the statute itself)

The primary text beneath the whole report: §101(a)(43)’s aggravated-felony definition and §101(a)(13)’s admission rules, §212’s inadmissibility grounds and the §212(a)(9) bars, §237’s deportability grounds, and §316’s naturalization requirements. Every section of the desk’s report is a reading of this book.

Subjective
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement — Fiscal Year 2024 Annual Report, December 19, 2024

The agency’s own yearbook: 271,484 removals, 88,763 of them (32.7 percent) of persons with criminal histories; 113,431 arrests; 47,732 interior removals running 93 percent criminal-involved; the non-detained docket above 7.6 million. The spine of sections 4 and 12.

Subjective
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement — FY 2013 Immigration Removals report, and the FY 2015 end-of-year statistics

The baseline years of the criminal-share series: 368,644 removals in fiscal 2013, 59 percent convicted overall and 82 percent convicted among interior removals; the interior convicted share at 91 percent by fiscal 2015. Printed with the agency’s stated priority framework of the period.

Subjective
Department of Homeland Security — Entry/Exit Overstay Report, Fiscal Year 2024

The overstay census: 46,657,108 expected departures, 538,548 overstay events, a 1.15 percent total rate; Mexico, Colombia, India, and Canada the largest counts; visa-waiver states at 0.43 percent, students at 2.45 percent. The source document of section 7.

Subjective
Department of Homeland Security, Office of Homeland Security Statistics — Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, Table 42 (removals by criminal status, region, and nationality)

The nationality ledger of section 7’s companion count: 183,360 formal removals in fiscal 2023, of whom 1,540 were European—Spain 160 against 18,192 suspected Spanish overstays, the United Kingdom 170 against 13,816.

Subjective
Government Accountability Office — GAO-21-487, “Immigration Enforcement: ICE Can Improve Monitoring of Noncitizen Interests,” July 2021

The auditors’ error file: 674 arrests, 121 detentions, and 70 removals of potential United States citizens across fiscal 2015 to mid-2020, detainers issued against at least 895 more, and a finding that ICE’s citizenship-claim records are too inconsistent for the counts to be more than floors. Section 13 rests on it.

Subjective
TRAC Immigration, Syracuse University — detention and court quick facts, 2026

The independent tabulations of the government’s own released data: 65,765 persons in detention on July 11, 2026, 70.6 percent without a criminal conviction; 3,037,800 cases pending in immigration court at the end of September 2026; 2,840 persons wrongly flagged removable between 2002 and 2017 in the earlier study. The counters beside the agency’s.

Subjective
Congressional Research Service — report IF13208, April 24, 2026

The legislative branch’s ledger: the non-detained docket at 7.3 million in February 2026 with an estimated 1.6 million final orders; immigration judges’ 485,456 removal orders in fiscal 2025, 306,557 in absentia. Filed for the scale section’s docket figures.

Subjective
Austin Kocher — reconstruction of ICE removals from the agency’s biweekly releases, fiscal 2025

The researcher’s rebuild of the year the agency did not summarize in an annual report at filing: 329,018 ERO removals for fiscal 2025, against USAFacts’ 320,000. Filed beside the official series with its method stated, as the desk files all reconstructions.

Subjective
David J. Bier, Cato Institute — analysis of ICE detention bookings, November 2025

The libertarian institute’s reading of ICE’s own booking data: 73 percent of persons booked into detention as of November 2025 had no criminal conviction; 5 percent had a violent conviction. Filed as the critics’ arithmetic, checked against the agency’s releases it derives from.

Subjective
Department of Homeland Security — press releases on departures and “self-deportation,” October and December 2025

The department’s claims in its own words: 1.6 million self-deportations announced in October 2025, 1.9 million by December, and 622,000 deportations since January 20, 2025. The methodology is not published with them; the desk files the claims and the absence together, in section 5 and the ledger.

Subjective
Deportation Data Project, via Stateline — voluntary departure grants, January–July 2025

The counted counterweight to the self-deportation claim: 6,118 grants of voluntary departure recorded in the courts’ data between January 20 and July 29, 2025. Filed beside the department’s releases, as the shelf files claim and count together.

Subjective
Leocal v. Ashcroft, 543 U.S. 1 (2004); Matter of Lopez-Meza, 22 I&N Dec. 1188 (BIA 1999); Matter of Castillo-Perez, 27 I&N Dec. 664 (A.G. 2019)

The drunk-driving trilogy of section 3: DUI is not a crime of violence and so not an aggravated felony; ordinary DUI is not moral turpitude, though the knowing-unlicensed variant was held to be; two or more DUIs raise a presumption against good moral character. Together they state the current law the pending bill would displace.

Subjective
Congress.gov — H.R. 875, the Protect Our Communities from DUIs Act, 119th Congress

The pending text and its path: passed the House June 26, 2025, by 246 to 160; referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee June 27, 2025; no further action recorded at filing. The bill would add DUI—conviction or admission—to both the inadmissibility and deportability lists, without waiver or misdemeanor exception.

Subjective
Padilla v. Kentucky, 559 U.S. 356 (2010); Chaidez v. United States, 568 U.S. 342 (2013); Sessions v. Dimaya, 584 U.S. 148 (2018)

The plea-room cases of section 8 and the definition case of section 3: counsel must advise on deportation consequences that are clear; the duty is not retroactive; and the residual “crime of violence” clause is void for vagueness, narrowing the aggravated-felony term to its element-based core.

Subjective
Public Law 104-218, 110 Stat. 3021 (October 1, 1996); U.S. Department of State, 8 FAM 306.1

The honorary-citizenship file of section 9: the act conferring honorary citizenship on Mother Teresa, one of eight such grants and one of two to a living recipient; and the manual’s plain statement that the honor confers no entry, travel, or immigration benefit and no passport eligibility.

Subjective
Center for Migration Studies — the overstay-majority studies; Pew Research Center, unauthorized population estimates, 2025

The flow and stock estimates of section 7: overstays exceeding entries without inspection among new unauthorized residents every year since about 2007 (CMS), and the unauthorized population estimated at about 14 million in 2023 (Pew). Filed as estimates, with their residual method, wherever the report uses them.

Subjective
European Commission — the Schengen short-stay rules (Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 and the Visa Code)

The comparative ledger’s primary text: ninety days in any 180-day period, counted on a rolling basis; the membership list that places Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland inside the area and the United Kingdom and Ireland outside it. Section 6’s cumulative-clock ruling rests on it.

Subjective
Abrego Garcia v. Noem, No. 8:25-cv-00951 (D. Md.) — the Cerna declaration of March 31, 2025, and the orders of April 2025; Immigration Policy Tracking Project docket

The error file’s central case in its own documents: the agency’s sworn statement that the removal was an administrative error, the district court’s facilitation order, the Supreme Court’s April 10, 2025 disposition, and the return into criminal custody that followed.

Subjective
Commission on Presidential Debates — transcript of the third presidential debate, Las Vegas, October 19, 2016

The “bad hombres” passage in its full sentence, with the two-part promise around it—first acts against the drug lords and “bad ones,” a later determination for “the rest”—filed as the specimen text of section 11.

Subjective
Theresa Cardinal Brown, Center for a New American Security — “Unintended Consequences,” on the ICE surge (ERO staffing baseline); USAFacts, immigration judges count, 2026

The staffing exhibits of section 12: ERO’s roughly 6,100 deportation officers before the 2025 expansion, the $75 billion appropriation and the hiring it funds; and the bench count—557 immigration judges, down from 735 at the fiscal 2024 peak—against the backlog the bench carries.

entry.title: Election Integrity in America: Voting, Mail-In Ballots, and the Theft Claims of 2016, 2020, 2024, and 2026
entry.summary: How American elections run end to end, the documented record of election fraud from the machine era to the present, the mail-ballot turn of 2020, and the theft claims of 2016, 2020, 2024, and 2026 tested by one instrument: cause, manner, baseline. The whole record, attributed.
entry.content:
Special Report

The Election File — Voting, Counting, and the Claims

Objective

Election Integrity in America: Voting, Mail-In Ballots, and the Theft Claims of 2016, 2020, 2024, and 2026

American elections are run by thousands of local offices under fifty state systems, and the documented record of fraud in them is real, old, and small against the count: 1,619 proven cases in the most-cited database across forty-three years and roughly 2.26 billion federal ballots. Four consecutive national elections have now drawn theft claims, from four different directions, and none of the four has produced evidence that changed a certified result. The desk files the machinery, the history, the modern turn, and the four claims, each tested by the same instrument.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0910 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026.

The File in Brief

The desk has no stake in any election in this file, and this report is written from that position: no party, no candidate, no preferred outcome for 2028, and no claim excluded from examination because it sits outside the respectable shelf. On the verified record: American elections are administered by states and counties, not by any national authority; a ballot passes through registration, casting, counting, canvass, and certification, and each stage carries its own verification instrument—signature and database checks at registration, paper records and post-election audits at counting, public canvass and court contests after. Fraud is a documented American tradition with named practitioners: the machine-era stuffing of the nineteenth century, the disputed count of 1876, the confessed theft of a Texas Senate primary in 1948, and a modern case file that runs to overturned elections in North Carolina in 2018 and Connecticut in 2023, each produced by absentee-ballot schemes, each small, each prosecuted or voided through the system’s own machinery. The largest single change in the modern record arrived in 2020, when the pandemic moved 46 percent of all votes to the mail; parts of that emergency settlement became permanent law, and the argument over it has not closed. The theft claims of the last decade were tested by the same instruments in each cycle. In 2016, a bipartisan Senate committee and the intelligence community documented a Russian interference operation and found no evidence that vote tallies were changed; recounts in three states moved margins by hundreds of votes. In 2020, more than sixty lawsuits failed, hand recounts and a court-adjacent audit in the two most-contested states affirmed the certified results, and the Attorney General of the United States stated that his department had found no fraud that would change the outcome. In 2024, theft claims ran in both directions—against the winner from the left, and pre-emptively for him from the right—and the certification proceeded without a successful contest. In 2026, the losing side’s theft claims have so far been limited and social-media-borne, defeated candidates of the president’s party have largely conceded, and the one large numerical argument now circulating—26,185,294 new registrations in 2022–2024, 20,283,937 of them in states without documentary proof-of-citizenship requirements—is a true count of registration records drawn from the Election Assistance Commission’s own survey, carrying a conclusion the survey does not contain. The questions that remain live for 2028 are narrower than the argument around them: noncitizen voting, documented by state audits at rates between zero and a few thousand flagged records per state against rolls in the millions, with confirmed ballots in the tens per state where they are confirmed at all; ballot collection, lawful in most states in some form and criminal in a few, with its abuse cases documented and punished; and a federal proof-of-citizenship statute, the SAVE Act and its successor, that has passed the House twice and has not become law. The operative events in every dispute are certification and seating, and the remedies run on statutory clocks measured in days. The ledger at the end of this report sorts the whole subject into four columns—verified, documented-but-small, claimed-but-unproven, and disproven—and every claim in the file, including the claim that elections are staged by hidden powers, is filed in one of them.

1. The Record: How American Elections Actually Run

There is no American election; there are fifty state elections and thousands of county ones, run simultaneously on the same day. The Constitution assigns the times, places, and manner of federal elections to state legislatures, subject to Congress’s power to alter those regulations; the machinery below that grant is local. Counties and municipalities register voters, print ballots, staff polling places, operate drop boxes, receive mail ballots, tabulate, and report. State officials—secretaries of state, state boards—set rules, maintain the statewide registration database each state has kept since the Help America Vote Act of 2002, canvass the county returns, and certify. The federal role is bounded: the Election Assistance Commission certifies voting-system standards and surveys the whole apparatus after each cycle; the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency advises on security; the Justice Department enforces the federal voting statutes; Congress counts the electoral votes and, since the Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022, does so under rules that make the state-certified slate the operative one. The consequence for every claim in this file is structural: a national election has no single point at which it can be seized, and no single custodian whose corruption settles it. It has roughly ten thousand jurisdictions whose results must agree, in public, with the paper and the counts beneath them.

Registration is the first gate, and it runs on attestation backed by database checks, not on documents produced at the door. A federal registration form, and the state forms modeled on it, requires the applicant to state name, address, and date of birth, to supply a driver’s-license number or the last four digits of a Social Security number, and to swear—under penalty of perjury—that the applicant is a United States citizen and meets the state’s requirements. The state then matches the application against motor-vehicle and Social Security records; a failed match does not complete a registration until the discrepancy is resolved. A small number of states additionally require documentary proof of citizenship, and the legal fight over that requirement is a live question in section 5 of this report. Registration is not a one-time act but a maintained list: under the National Voter Registration Act, states run a general program to remove the dead, the moved, and the otherwise ineligible, under a rule that bars systematic removals within ninety days of a federal election. The Election Assistance Commission’s 2024 survey counted 103,512,313 registration transactions in the 2022–2024 window and 21,298,175 records removed in the same period—the rolls churn by tens of millions between cycles as a matter of ordinary administration.

Casting now takes four principal forms, and the shares moved sharply in 2020 and partly back. A voter may vote in person on Election Day; in person early, in the states that offer it; by mail, on request in most states and automatically in the universal vote-by-mail states; or by mail ballot returned in person, to an election office, a polling place, or a drop box. The MIT Election Lab’s survey of the 2020 election measured the settlement at its most mail-heavy: 46 percent of votes cast by mail, against 21 percent in 2016, and Election Day in-person voting down from 60 percent to 28 percent. The Postal Service handled roughly 135 million pieces of election mail between September 1 and November 3, 2020. Of mail ballots returned in 2020, about 22 percent nationally came back through drop boxes; in Colorado, Oregon, and Washington, the long-standing all-mail states, the drop-box share was about 60 percent. Each form carries its own check: in-person voting against the poll book; mail voting against the registration record, by signature comparison on the return envelope in most states, by witness or notary requirements in a few, and by ballot-tracking systems in a growing number.

Counting is a public, layered process, and its last stages are the ones that decide disputes. Precinct and central-count tabulators produce results that are reported unofficially on election night; nothing about election night is final. The canvass follows: county boards reconcile ballots cast against voters checked in, account for provisional and cured ballots, and certify county results to the state; the state canvasses and certifies the statewide result, for presidential elections under the federal calendar that the Electoral Count Reform Act reset—state certification in time for electors to meet in December, Congress to count on January 6. Post-election audits sit between counting and certification in most states, from fixed-percentage hand counts of batches to risk-limiting audits that sample ballots until the reported outcome is confirmed to a stated statistical standard. Recounts, automatic under state thresholds or available on request, rerun the tabulation and, where the record is paper, can rerun the ballots themselves. Contests move the question to courts or, for congressional seats, to the House and Senate, which judge the elections of their own members. The operative events—the points at which a claim becomes a result or dies—are certification by the state and seating by the chamber. Everything before them is evidence; those two acts are the election.

The verification instruments are concrete and were built, mostly, out of documented failures. Paper records exist for the overwhelming majority of American votes cast since the post-2000 reforms and the paper-trail movement described in section 3, which is what makes hand recounts and audits physically possible. Chain-of-custody rules govern ballots and equipment; bipartisan teams handle ballots in the contested counts; observers from both parties and the public may watch canvasses and recounts in every state. Logic-and-accuracy testing of tabulators is conducted in public before elections. None of this makes fraud impossible, and section 2 records the cases where it happened anyway. What the instruments determine is the size of fraud that can hide: a scheme must survive the paper, the reconciliation of ballots to voters, the observation, and the audit, and the documented schemes in the modern record were caught by exactly those instruments—by canvass officials who refused to certify, by voters who reported ballots collected and never delivered, and by surveillance and signature records examined after the fact.

2. The History: Fraud as a Documented American Tradition

The category “stolen election” has a factual floor, and the floor is old. In the machine era, ballot stuffing was not an allegation but a method of government in the cities that ran on it. New York’s Tammany Hall under William M. Tweed naturalized immigrants in mass proceedings timed to elections, repeated voters under false names, and counted returns its own inspectors wrote; the Tweed Ring’s theft of public money was prosecuted in the 1870s and Tweed died in jail in 1878. Samuel J. Tilden made his name prosecuting that machine—and then, as the Democratic presidential nominee of 1876, stood at the center of the election that remains the republic’s closest approach to a settled-by-procedure theft. Tilden won the popular vote outright, 4,288,546 to 4,034,311, the only candidate in American history to lose while holding a majority of it, and stood at 184 electoral votes, one short, with twenty votes disputed from Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and Oregon against a background of documented violence and intimidation aimed at Black Republican voters across the South. Congress built an Electoral Commission of fifteen; it voted 8 to 7, on party lines, on every question, and awarded all twenty votes to Rutherford B. Hayes, who won 185 to 184. The settlement that ended the crisis, the Compromise of 1877, withdrew federal troops from the South and closed Reconstruction. The desk files 1876 as the standing exhibit of what a disputed American election actually looks like when the machinery is the prize: competing returns, a tribunal built for the occasion, a decision on partisan lines, and a price paid in policy for acceptance of the result.

The confessed cases are the floor’s strongest boards, because the practitioners themselves supplied the evidence. In the 1948 Texas Democratic primary for the United States Senate, Lyndon B. Johnson defeated former governor Coke Stevenson by 87 votes after Box 13 in Jim Wells County produced 202 late ballots, alphabetically ordered, in the same hand and ink, nearly all for Johnson. In 1977, Luis Salas, the election judge who had certified those ballots, told the Associated Press that he had certified two hundred fraudulent votes on the order of George B. Parr, the political boss of Duval County: “Johnson did not win the election; it was stolen for him. And I know exactly how it was done.” The federal courts declined to undo the result in 1948, Johnson was seated, and the confession stands in the record unrebutted. The method matters to the present file: the theft was retail, local, executed by the officials who ran one county’s count, and visible in the physical record—the handwriting and the alphabetical order—to anyone who examined the ballots. In 1888, the national Republican campaign’s treasurer, William W. Dudley, was caught in writing instructing Indiana operatives to buy voters in “blocks of five”; Indiana went for Benjamin Harrison by a margin the purchased blocks were sized to cover, and the letter, not a recount, is the evidence. Vote-buying at retail was so ordinary in the nineteenth century that its exposure caused scandal mainly for the candor.

1960 is the century’s contested case, and its record is charges, evidence of irregularities, and no adjudicated reversal. John F. Kennedy defeated Richard Nixon by about 118,000 popular votes out of some 68 million; Illinois went to Kennedy by 8,858 votes and Texas by about 46,000, and flipping both would have elected Nixon. The charges centered on Chicago, where Mayor Richard J. Daley’s organization was documented then and since to have produced votes by methods that included the dead and the fictitious, and on South Texas, where the Parr machine’s methods were already a matter of confession in the 1948 case. Republican challenges and recount efforts in multiple states produced no reversal of any state’s result; Hawaii’s recount, the one completed statewide exercise, moved that state from Nixon to Kennedy. Nixon conceded and, as vice president, presided over the counting of Kennedy’s electoral votes. Historians continue to argue the Illinois evidence; what the procedural record holds is that no court or canvass found outcome-changing fraud, the remedies available were attempted, and the result certified stood. The year 2000 supplied the modern template instead: Florida decided the presidency by 537 certified votes, the contest ran through recounts and courts for thirty-six days, and the Supreme Court’s decision in Bush v. Gore ended the recount and with it the contest. The desk notes the sequence because it is the standard against which later claims are measured: 2000 is what an election inside the margin of litigation looks like—weeks of public process, named judges, printed orders, and a loser who conceded the day after the ruling.

The modern case file is specific, prosecuted, and dominated by one instrument: the absentee ballot. In Clay County, Kentucky, eight local officials, among them a judge and a school superintendent, were convicted in federal court for a scheme run across the 2002–2006 cycles that bought votes and manipulated absentee ballots to hold county offices. In the 2018 congressional election in North Carolina’s 9th district, operative Leslie McCrae Dowless ran what the State Board of Elections found to be a coordinated, unlawful, and substantially resourced absentee-ballot scheme for the Republican candidate: paid workers were compensated per batch of absentee-ballot request forms collected and per batch of ballots collected, some ballots were completed or discarded by the operation, and the board—on the evidence of the operation’s own scale in a race decided by 905 votes—refused to certify and ordered a new election. Dowless and seven others were indicted; Dowless died in April 2022 awaiting trial; the candidate was not charged and did not run in the new election, which the other party won. In Bridgeport, Connecticut, in 2023, a Democratic mayoral primary decided by 251 votes was overturned after surveillance video showed a party official and others depositing multiple absentee ballots into drop boxes; the trial judge wrote that the court was “unable to determine the legitimate result,” ordered a new primary, and criminal charges followed against eleven people by late 2025. In Aberdeen, Mississippi, a judge’s 64-page order found irregularities in 66 of 84 absentee ballots in a 2020 local race decided by 37 votes, and ordered a new election. Across the longer run, researchers count at least fourteen elections invalidated between 1978 and 2018 specifically for absentee-ballot fraud, twelve of them local, and none overturned for voter impersonation in the same span. The floor, stated as a rate: the Heritage Foundation’s database, the largest public compilation of proven cases, lists 1,619 proven instances of election fraud from 1982 to 2025, about 1,380 of them ending in criminal conviction, against roughly 2.26 billion ballots cast in the federal general elections of that period—on the order of seven proven cases per ten million ballots. The Foundation itself describes the database as a sampling that does not capture all cases, and the desk prints that caveat with the figure: the true incidence is higher than the proven count and unmeasured; the proven count is the floor, and it is a floor of thousands of cases against billions of ballots.

3. The Modern Turn: Technology, Mail Ballots, and the 2020 Settlement

The modern era of election administration begins with a counting failure on live television and the statute it produced. The 2000 Florida recount exposed punch-card ballots, ambiguous marks, and county-level inconsistency to the whole country; the Help America Vote Act of 2002 answered with money for new voting systems, statewide computerized registration databases, and provisional ballots. The first technology wave that followed—touchscreen direct-recording electronic machines with no paper record—produced its own documented problem: in several jurisdictions, malfunctioning or unverifiable machines left results that could not be independently recounted, and computer scientists demonstrated, in laboratory conditions, that the leading systems could be compromised. The paper-trail movement that answered it is the reason the modern count can be audited at all: state after state required a voter-verifiable paper record, the purely electronic machines were retired, and by 2020 the overwhelming majority of American votes were cast on paper ballots or machines producing paper records. The standing lesson the desk draws from the sequence is narrow and factual: each generation of equipment created the verification question its successor was built to answer, and the current settlement—paper, audits, public testing—is the third iteration, not the first design.

Voter identification law spread over the same decades and is now the background condition of in-person voting in most states. The National Conference of State Legislatures’ tracker counts 35 states with some form of identification law for in-person voting: seven classified as strict photo ID, under which a ballot does not count unless the voter completes additional steps, and 28 with non-strict or non-photo requirements, under which alternatives—a signed affidavit, a utility record, a poll worker’s vouching, a provisional ballot counted after verification—keep the ballot in the count. Mail voting carries its own identity instruments in place of the polling-place check: the application is matched to the registration record, the returned envelope is signature-checked in most states, and specific states require a witness signature, a notary, or an identification number on the envelope instead. The contested empirical question—how many eligible voters such laws turn away, against how much fraud they prevent—is argued from the same two datasets by both sides and is filed in the ledger below as an open measurement dispute, not resolved here, because the record located does not resolve it.

The mail-ballot expansion of 2020 was an emergency construction, and its parts had different fates. Before 2020, five states—Colorado, Hawaii, Oregon, Utah, and Washington—conducted elections principally by mail, sending ballots to every registered voter as standard procedure. In 2020, under pandemic authority, California, the District of Columbia, New Jersey, Nevada, and Vermont joined them for that cycle, Montana left the choice to counties, and most remaining states expanded no-excuse absentee access, extended deadlines, or added drop boxes and prepaid return postage at a speed no ordinary legislative session would have produced. The count that resulted was the largest mail vote in American history: 46 percent of all ballots, roughly 66 million postal ballots, and a Postal Service operation of about 135 million election-mail pieces. The emergency also generated the era’s signature disputes in real time: a Texas proclamation limiting each county to one ballot drop-off location, a California dispute over unofficial Republican drop-off boxes, litigation over receipt deadlines and signature rules in dozens of states. What became permanent, state by state, is the present map: eight states now mail every voter a ballot as standing law; no-excuse absentee is available in about two-thirds of the states; drop boxes are expressly authorized and regulated in roughly half the states, restricted or prohibited in others; and the receipt rule splits—35 states require the ballot in hand by Election Day, while 15 states and the District of Columbia count ballots postmarked by Election Day and received later. The desk prints the map as the trackers give it, dated August 2025 to September 2026, because state legislatures continue to move the lines.

Ballot collection—third parties returning other voters’ ballots—is the practice where the modern argument and the documented fraud record physically meet. As of September 2026, Ballotpedia’s state-by-state compilation counts 28 states and the District of Columbia permitting any person the voter chooses to return the ballot, 16 states permitting return by persons with specified relationships to the voter, 4 states permitting only the voter to return it with exceptions, and 2 states requiring return by mail. Layered over that map: 15 states limit the number of ballots one person may return, 12 states bar specified persons such as candidates from collecting, and 3 restrict paying collectors. The documented abuse cases in section 2—North Carolina 2018, Bridgeport 2023—were collection schemes: operatives gathered ballots from voters’ hands, which is why the practice, lawful assistance in most of the country and a felony in tightly drawn circumstances in some of it, carries the argument’s weight. Registration itself has also been mechanized at the front end: automatic voter registration, under which eligible citizens are registered through motor-vehicle and other agency transactions unless they decline, operates in about half the states in some form; and list maintenance has been mechanized at the back end, principally through the Electronic Registration Information Center, founded in 2012 by seven states with Pew Charitable Trusts support, which matches member states’ voter and motor-vehicle data to flag movers, duplicates, and the dead, and which about a third of states have left since 2023 amid criticism—filed below, attributed—of its outreach requirements and the confidentiality of its reports. The United States consequently runs its elections on a registration and counting infrastructure that is simultaneously more automated and more contested than the one it replaced.

4. The Four Claims: 2016, 2020, 2024, 2026

The desk applies one instrument to all four elections: the stated cause of the alleged theft, the manner in which it was to have been executed, the baseline against which its size is measured, and the evidence each side produced. A theft claim that cannot name a manner fails the instrument before it reaches evidence; a claim whose manner is named is tested against the audits, recounts, and court records that the manner would have left behind. The four claims are filed in chronological order and in identical form.

2016: The Interference Finding and the Recounts

Cause and manner, as claimed. The 2016 theft claim, made principally from the Democratic side after Hillary Clinton’s defeat, held in its strong form that Russian interference had stolen the election, and in its narrower forms that Russian operations, the FBI director’s late letter, and voter-suppression laws in Republican states had together moved a margin measured in tens of thousands of votes across Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. The documented interference is not in dispute as to its existence: the January 2017 intelligence community assessment judged that Russia ran a coherent influence campaign—hack-and-leak operations against Democratic targets and a social-media operation through the Internet Research Agency—aimed at harming Clinton, and the bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee, after its own multi-year investigation, confirmed the campaign and found Russian scanning or probing of election infrastructure touching all fifty states. The same committee record holds the limiting finding: no evidence was found that vote tallies were changed or that voting machines were hacked to change them. Jill Stein’s recount petitions tested the count itself in the three closest states. In Wisconsin, the completed statewide recount changed the result by 0.06 percent: Donald Trump’s margin grew by a net 162 votes. In Michigan, courts halted the recount after ruling Stein, who took about one percent of the vote, was not an aggrieved candidate positioned to change the outcome; the certified margin was under 11,000 votes of 4.8 million. In Pennsylvania, a federal judge rejected the recount request; the certified margin was about 44,000 of six million. Clinton had conceded the morning after the election. On the instrument: interference—verified, documented by two branches of the United States government and its closest allies’ services; vote alteration—no specimen produced, and the recounts that could have produced one moved the count by hundreds. The claim as stated in its strong form is filed as disproven as to tallies and verified as to interference; the weaker proposition, that interference changed enough minds to change the outcome, is not measurable by any instrument that exists and is filed as unproven by construction.

2020: The Litigation, the Recounts, and the Certificates

Cause and manner, as claimed. The 2020 claim, made by President Trump and his allies after Joseph Biden’s victory, held that coordinated fraud—mail ballots cast in the names of the dead and the ineligible, ballots counted after observers were excluded, voting machines switching votes, late-night ballot deliveries—had stolen five or six close states and with them the presidency. The certified margins it had to overcome were 10,457 votes in Arizona, 11,779 in Georgia, and 20,682 in Wisconsin. The claims were tested in every forum the system provides. More than sixty lawsuits brought by the campaign and its allies were dismissed or lost, on evidence, standing, or procedure, including before judges appointed by the president making the claim; the Supreme Court declined to hear the largest of them, Texas’s suit against four other states, in December 2020. Attorney General William Barr stated in December 2020 that the Justice Department had not found fraud on a scale that would change the outcome; the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s joint statement called the election the most secure in American history. Georgia conducted a full hand recount of its roughly five million ballots, which reaffirmed Biden’s victory, and then a machine recount, which did so again. Wisconsin’s recount in its two largest counties, paid for by the Trump campaign at about $3 million, increased Biden’s lead by 87 votes. In Arizona, the state Senate’s commissioned review by Cyber Ninjas, conducted outside the official canvass, hand-counted Maricopa County’s ballots and reported more votes for Biden than the certified count—a net of roughly 360 additional Biden votes in its tally. A group of conservative lawyers and former officials, examining the claims case by case in the report Lost, Not Stolen, found no evidence that fraud altered the outcome. The Associated Press’s review of the six disputed battleground states identified fewer than 475 potential fraud cases among more than 25 million ballots cast in them—potential cases, referred for investigation, against margins in those states that began above ten thousand votes each. Documented fraud did occur in 2020, at the scale the floor in section 2 predicts: individual prosecutions for double voting, ballots cast for deceased relatives, and the Aberdeen, Mississippi absentee case among them. On the instrument: the manner alleged was industrial in scale and would have left evidence in the paper; the paper was recounted by hand in the two states where the allegation concentrated, and it answered the other way. The outcome-changing claim is filed as disproven by recount, audit, and adjudication; small-scale fraud is filed as documented; the fake-elector episode is filed separately below because it is a different category of act.

The alternate certificates are a documented act with a documented legal aftermath, not a fraud claim. In December 2020, Republican electors in seven states Biden had won signed and transmitted alternate certificates of electoral votes. The ensuing prosecutions ran state by state and, as of late 2026, stand as follows on the reporting assembled: Georgia’s case unraveled after the district attorney’s disqualification in December 2024, one defendant—attorney Kenneth Chesebro—having pleaded guilty in October 2023; Michigan’s charges against fifteen electors were dismissed in 2025 and the attorney general declined to appeal; Nevada’s charges were dismissed twice, the second dismissal resting on a 2026 ruling that the state’s forgery statutes do not reach openly transmitted conduct, with the attorney general announcing an appeal and the governor having twice vetoed a legislative remedy; Arizona’s attorney general dismissed her own prosecution in June 2026 to restart a grand-jury process after courts found the original indictment defective; Wisconsin’s case against the scheme’s organizers, as distinct from the electors, was ruled in December 2025 fit for trial on felony forgery charges and stands as the one prosecution on track. Federal charges were dropped after the 2024 election under Justice Department policy, and federal pardons issued in November 2025 covered the participants’ federal exposure only. One partisan tally holds that no defendant has been convicted on the core fake-elector charges; the desk files that tally as an attributed claim, not a finding. The episode’s procedural meaning is fixed by the statute it produced: the Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022 raised the threshold for congressional objections, restricted the vice president’s role to the ministerial, and made the governor-certified slate the operative one—the system’s own answer, enacted, to the manner attempted.

2024: Claims in Both Directions

The 2024 cycle was the most litigated in American history before a vote was counted, and the theft claims afterward ran in both directions. Roughly 300 election lawsuits were filed in the cycle by one accounting; the parties’ pre-election suits contested registration rules, mail-ballot procedures, and machine certification across the battlegrounds. After Donald Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris, the claims from the losing side took three principal forms. The statistical form argued from anomalies: a University of Michigan statistician’s analyses were circulated as estimating tens of thousands of “unnatural” votes in Pennsylvania; the desk files that figure as an attributed claim whose published range within the same analysis runs from 29,000 to 225,000, a spread that itself measures the method’s uncertainty.
