And that begins with decisively addressing the affordability crisis.” The same account records the to-do list the majority says it will begin with—reversing the Medicaid changes in the president’s tax-and-spending law and restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that lapsed at the end of last year—and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer’s stated priorities: lowering the cost of living, cleaning up corruption in government, acting as a check on the administration, and using the annual government funding bills to impose limits on the administration and on the war in Iran. On impeachment, Jeffries repeated the sentence he has given every questioner: “I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment. We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability.” The account states the arithmetic both sides are working from: the majority will not hold veto-proof margins, so any major legislation will need the president’s signature. The program and the veto are now both on paper. What they produce together is the work of the Congress that convenes on January 3.

The Republican Party’s internal business for the week is a leadership election, and its date is set. The Daily Caller’s account records that Speaker Mike Johnson announced on Wednesday that he will not seek a leadership role in the next Congress, and that Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan launched bids the same day to become the party’s next leader. House Republicans hold their leadership elections on Tuesday, November 10, with candidates required to declare by November 6; Majority Whip Tom Emmer has told colleagues he will run for whip in the minority, and Republican Study Committee chairman August Pfluger is challenging him for that post, per the accounts filed below. Scalise’s letter to the conference, quoted in the Caller, states his case in one sentence: “I am ready to lead on day one and chart our path back to the majority.” In the Senate, Republicans hold their leadership elections on November 10 as well, and Majority Leader John Thune is expected to run again, per the accounts. Jeffries made his own bid for the speakership official in a Dear Colleague letter on Wednesday. The gavels change hands in January; the contests for who will hold the minority’s are decided next week.

The World at Evening

The foreign responses filed by evening sort into the same three groups as Wednesday’s, with the positions now stated by governments rather than parties. Al Jazeera’s roundup of the world’s reactions leads with Tehran: parliament speaker Ghalibaf’s post—“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message”—and the supreme leader’s statement that partisan shifts in Washington will not alter American hostility towards Iran. In Europe, European Parliament vice president Christel Schaldemose said the results left her “cautiously optimistic on Europe’s behalf”; Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called the Democratic victory emblematic of the unravelling of the global far right; Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the results presented an opportunity for world leaders to work together to ease cost-of-living pressures and resolve the conflict in the Middle East, per the account of the foreign leaders’ responses filed below; France’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, said Paris would wait to see whether the president, who remains in control of American foreign policy, adjusts his approach. Russia’s deputy foreign minister, Sergey Ryabkov, noted that the Democratic Party’s leaders had a sharply negative approach to relations with Moscow, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow hoped the results would not impact the president’s peacemaking efforts. South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said the election marks a new era in world relations. Japan’s chief cabinet secretary, Minoru Kihara, emphasized that the Japan–United States alliance stands. In Israel, where the prime minister’s coalition lost its own parliamentary majority last week, there was no immediate reaction from Benjamin Netanyahu; Yair Golan, of a coalition seeking to replace him, said the American vote reveals how toxic Netanyahu has become among American Democrats and Republicans alike. Every capital read the same election. Each read it as a sentence about itself, and the desk files the readings as readings.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the House: 248 seats won and 13 led in the Associated Press tracker’s latest state, 252 called for the Democrats in a live file updated at 2:44 p.m., and 247 projected in the Independent’s file at its hour—three call desks, three hours, one chamber, and agreement only on the outcome. Second, Colorado’s 4th: a margin of 2,513 votes in the wire and Decision Desk figures carried at midday, and 2,254 in the state’s figures in the afternoon file—the leader the same, the margin narrowing as the count proceeds, the race uncalled in both. Third, the strait: five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in the British agency’s count, two tankers on mines and a third on fire in the Revolutionary Guards’ Thursday statement, and two tankers and a tugboat on fire in the same statement as carried in a second file—the incidents claimed, the details unmatched, the confirmation absent. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the evening are single-valued: no Senate race was called on Thursday; the Dow closed down 1,833 points and the Nasdaq Composite down 5.52 percent, in correction; the semiconductor index fell about twelve percent; Brent settled at $98.29, up $3.67; initial jobless claims stand at 189,000, the lowest since 1969; the Bank of England’s rate stands at 4 percent; the House Republican leadership election is set for November 10; and Friday’s employment report is due at 8:30 a.m. The count belongs to the clerks until November 10 in Mississippi and November 18 in Alaska. The log proceeds to midnight.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-three items.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska and Mississippi both too early to call, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
Associated Press — House balance of power

248 House seats won by Democrats and 13 more led, against 154 won and 20 led for Republicans, in the tracker’s latest state.

Subjective
Poliwave — the House live results file

Updated November 5 at 2:44 p.m. EST: 252 House seats called for Democrats and 160 for Republicans, 412 of 435 races called, with Colorado’s 4th still counting at 176,162 to 173,649.

Subjective
The Independent — the live file, Thursday

House races projected for the Democrats during the day, including Luz Rivas in California, Sam Forstag in Montana, and Shannon Taylor in Virginia, with a projected total of 247 Democrats to 147 Republicans at its hour, and the Senate at 54 to 44.

Subjective
Rocky Mountain Voice — Colorado, every race

The secretary of state’s figures, updated 1:11 p.m. MST: the 5th District called for Jessica Killin, the first Democrat to win it since 1972; the 4th District at Laubacher 176,427, Boebert 174,173, with twenty of twenty-one counties still counting.

Subjective
The Business Standard — why Alaska and Mississippi have not been called

Mississippi’s 1,138-vote margin, its November 10 and November 13 dates, no runoff in the procedure, and no automatic recount; Alaska’s mail windows and its November 18 ranked-choice tabulation.

Subjective
MarketSpeaker — the close, November 5

The closing levels: the Nasdaq 100 down 6.36 percent to 26,629.81, the Nasdaq Composite down 5.52 percent to 24,315.00, the S&P 500 down 4.36 percent to 7,353.73, and the Dow down 1,833.06 points to 51,523.06; the VIX at 28.09, up 69.1 percent; Nvidia down 9.3 percent, AMD down 17.3 percent, SanDisk down 22.3 percent; the ten-year yield down about six basis points to roughly 4.84 percent.

Subjective
Reuters, via Kitco — Wall Street slumps on chip losses

Qualcomm down 9 percent on the smartphone chip miss; the semiconductor index down 7.1 percent at its hour; IREN, Hut 8, and Applied Digital down between 6 and 11 percent; CoreWeave down 9.3 percent and Nebius down 13.4 percent; Dell down 10.5 percent; Tesla down 9.5 percent; the Swissquote analyst’s statement on scrutiny of the AI buildout; and Cleveland Fed President Hammack’s preference for a gradual rate-hike path.

Subjective
Reuters — the tech-stock rout, a market view

The semiconductor index down as much as 11 percent, its worst performance since March 2020, and the Nasdaq down as much as 5 percent; more than a dozen large technology stocks down by double digits; the ballot initiatives limiting data-center building named among the causes; the semiconductor index about 31 percent below its 52-week high, in a commentator’s figure.

Subjective
The Private Banker — the S&P 500’s worst day since April 2025

The S&P 500 down about 4.3 percent, its steepest one-day decline since April 2025; the Nasdaq Composite down 5.5 percent into correction territory, more than 10 percent below its October 6 record; the Dow down 1,833.06 points; and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 12.25 percent to 9,011.14.

Subjective
Reuters, via 941 The Duke — jobless claims at 57-year lows

Initial claims down 6,000 to 189,000 for the week ended October 31, against a forecast of 196,000, matching the lowest reading since 1969; continuing claims at 1.718 million; third-quarter productivity up at a 3.6 percent annualized rate against a forecast of 2.8 percent; and the statement that the claims report has no bearing on Friday’s October employment report.

Subjective
SquawkNews — the November 5 market LiveCast brief

The day’s running digest: the S&P 500 down 4.36 percent and the Nasdaq 100 down 6.36 percent; Richmond Fed President Barkin’s statements that inflation is the most important risk for the Fed right now, that the AI buildout has had an inflationary impact in the near term, that credit dynamics in the banking sector are reassuring at this point, and that he has no point of view on fiscal policy following the election.

Subjective
Reuters — the Bank of England raises rates

Bank Rate raised to 4 percent from 3.75 percent by 8–1, Catherine Mann voting for 4.25 percent; inflation expected to reach about 5 percent in the middle of next year and to return to target in the third quarter of 2028; Governor Bailey’s statement that the increase is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is resolved.

Subjective
Reuters, via LSE — Brent settles up over $3 after tanker attacks

New York, November 5: Brent settled up $3.67, or 3.88 percent, at $98.29 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate closed up $2.40, or 2.72 percent, at $90.52, after both fell more than 8 percent on Wednesday; five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in the UKMTO count; Eurasia Group’s revised odds—a deal at 10 percent, renewed strikes at 60 percent, a standoff at 30 percent; the Saudi alerts at Yanbu and the Houthi claim at Dammam; and Foreign Minister Araghchi’s calls with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts.

Subjective
Reuters, via The Business Standard — tankers hit in Hormuz

Iran reports three more tankers damaged in the strait on Thursday; the UKMTO count of at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday; Parliament Speaker Qalibaf’s answer to the vice president—“Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?”; the supreme leader’s statement against submission; the two unnamed sources on resumed strikes; and Qatar’s statement that the United States and Iran are reviewing proposals.

Subjective
AnewZ — tensions persist as Qatar pushes for a deal

Qatar’s mediation intensified; both governments reviewing the mediators’ proposals; the senior Iranian official’s statement that the sides remain far apart and that Tehran’s conditions must precede the strait’s reopening; the 36-hour expectation for responses, and the later statement that no fixed deadline exists.

Subjective
Reuters, via The Business Standard — Democrats vow to rein in the president

The incoming majority’s focus on affordability and accountability in Jeffries’s words; the president’s ballroom appearance and his veto sentence; the war acknowledged and stood by; the vice president’s post quoted; Governor DeSantis’s extinction-level description; Speaker Johnson’s decision not to lead his caucus next year; and the lame-duck funding measure ahead.

Subjective
LADbible — the president’s warning on impeachment

The president’s statements as reported: a third impeachment attempt would destroy the Democratic Party; he is not concerned, “not even a little bit”; the Democrats are not in control because he sends their bills back with a nice stamp veto; he does not want to spend two years vetoing everything; and he will work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for the country.

Subjective
RVA Magazine, carrying States Newsroom — how the majority deals with the president

Jeffries’s afternoon statement that Democrats are ready, willing, and able to find bipartisan common ground beginning with the affordability crisis; the Medicaid reversal and the Affordable Care Act credits at the head of the to-do list; Schumer’s priorities of living costs, corruption, and a check on the administration, with funding bills used to limit the war; Jeffries’s impeachment sentence repeated; and the statement that the majority will not hold veto-proof margins.

Subjective
Daily Caller — Scalise and Jordan for the top House Republican post

Speaker Johnson’s announcement that he will not seek a leadership role; Majority Leader Scalise’s and Chairman Jordan’s bids launched Wednesday; the face-off set for Tuesday’s leadership elections; and Scalise’s sentence that he is ready to lead on day one and chart the path back to the majority.

Subjective
Reuters — futures steady, Nasdaq lags

At 5:04 a.m. ET: Dow contracts up 0.48 percent, S&P 500 contracts up 0.01 percent, Nasdaq 100 contracts down 0.63 percent; Qualcomm down 10.1 percent premarket; the UBS note putting about 30 percent of expected 2028 data-center additions at risk; three Fed officials to speak, and Friday’s October jobs report ahead.

Subjective
Al Jazeera, via EuropeSays — “Seismic shift”: the world reacts

The world’s reactions as the scale of the victory emerged: Ghalibaf’s “NO TO WAR” post and the supreme leader’s answer; Schaldemose cautiously optimistic; Sánchez on the unravelling of the global far right; Britain’s health minister on steady ties through a seismic shift; France’s finance minister waiting on the president; Ryabkov on the Democrats and Moscow; Peskov’s hope for the peacemaking efforts; Ramaphosa’s new era; and Golan on Netanyahu.

Subjective
Fox News — the foreign leaders’ claims

The responses of foreign leaders who have clashed with the president: Sánchez’s post on the rejection of the president’s agenda; Schaldemose’s cautious optimism; Burnham on cost-of-living pressures and the Middle East conflict; Japan’s chief cabinet secretary on the alliance; Ramaphosa’s new era in world relations; and the president’s congratulations and veto warning printed with them.

entry.title: At Noon the Rally Turns: The Counts Hold, the Chips Fall, London Raises
entry.summary: The midday state of the count and the markets, November 5, 2026: no new Senate call, Mississippi's margin wider in the newest tally, the House counted four ways, Wall Street's second reading, oil back up, London raises, and the official statements. Edition No. 7, the Midday Watch.
entry.content:
The Midterm Elections — The Midday File

Objective

At Noon the Rally Turns: The Counts Hold, the Chips Fall, London Raises

The midday state of the count and the markets: no new Senate call, Mississippi’s margin wider in the newest tally, the House counted four ways, Wall Street’s second reading an hour into the session, oil back up, the Bank of England up a quarter point, and the official statements of the second morning.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Thursday, November 5, 2026. This edition corrects and continues Edition No. 6, the Overnight Watch, which stands unrevised, as a log stands. Where the noon count differs from the overnight count, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Noon Count

No race was called in the morning, in either chamber, in any state. The Senate stands where the overnight edition left it: 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled. The Associated Press Senate file in its latest state still lists both races as too early to call. Control of neither chamber is in question in any count on the shelf. The morning’s work was arithmetic at the edges, the markets’ second reading of a result they had already priced once, and the statements of the men and women who will have to govern with the result in January.

The House is counted four ways at noon, and the desk prints the spread. The Associated Press tracker carried in the overnight edition stood at 235 seats won by the Democrats and 26 led, against 146 won and 28 led for the Republicans. Ballotpedia’s Thursday accounting puts the called figure lower and the open figure higher: Democrats have gained at least 30 districts and hold at least a 233–138 majority in called races, with 64 races uncalled—12 in Democratic-held districts and 52 in Republican-held—and it carries Decision Desk HQ’s projection of a final 249 and NBC’s of 255. The live results file carrying Decision Desk HQ’s own totals, in its November 5 update, runs the called figure higher than either: 251 House seats called for the Democrats and 153 for the Republicans, with 31 still uncalled. A morning accounting checked against CBS News and Reuters carries an estimate of the end: a final Democratic total between 251 and 268. The tallies were taken at different hours from different call desks; they disagree about how much of the House has been called, and they agree about everything else. Ballotpedia’s measurement of the wave itself is printed for the record: the Senate’s net swing of at least seven seats against the president’s party meets its threshold for a wave election; the House’s net Republican loss of 26 seats so far does not meet its threshold of 48, and the uncalled races could still change that total. Democrats will hold 21 state trifectas, the most the party has held since 1992, per the same accounting.

Mississippi and Alaska: The Margins at Noon

Mississippi’s margin is wider in the newest tally than in the figure this paper carried overnight, and the leader is the same in every tally. The overnight edition, following the Associated Press figures in the explainer then on the shelf, carried the Democrat, Scott Colom, at 464,926 votes to the incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith’s 463,788—a margin of 1,138, with an estimated 96 percent counted. The Decision Desk HQ figures carried in the live file are newer and larger on both sides: Colom 466,464, Hyde-Smith 464,612, a margin of 1,852, in a source update timed November 4 at 6:38 p.m. EST; a later Decision Desk update carried in the same file’s state panel, timed November 5 at 14:01 UTC, puts the pair at 466,689 to 464,871, a margin of 1,818. A third tally, updated at 10:14 a.m. EST today, puts Colom at 466,246 and Hyde-Smith at 464,526, a margin of 1,720. The desk prints the range rather than a single figure: at noon Colom leads by somewhere between 1,138 and 1,852 votes depending on the tally and the hour it was taken, and the race is uncalled in all of them.

The procedure did not change in the morning. Mississippi does not require a majority in a regular federal general election; the candidate with the most votes wins, and there is no runoff—the correction this paper printed in Edition No. 6 stands. Approximately 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots remain to be received within five business days, and an unknown number of affidavit ballots remain to be processed, per Secretary of State Michael Watson’s statement carried in the live file. Affidavit identification is due by November 10; counties certify by November 13; the state holds no automatic recounts.

Alaska did not move at all. The Democrat, Mary Peltola, leads the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 first-choice votes—102,962 to 102,325—in the Decision Desk figures and in the Associated Press figures quoted in the live file this morning, and by 626 in the wire figures carried in the overnight explainer. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holds more votes than either margin. Both leaders are below 50 percent of first choices. Alaska accepts domestic mail ballots for up to 10 days after Election Day and overseas ballots for up to 15 days, provided they were mailed by November 3, and the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18. In the governorship the Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, holds 49.2 percent of first choices with about 74 percent counted, on the same November 18 schedule if no majority emerges.

Colorado and Kansas: No Move

Colorado’s 4th District stands exactly where the overnight edition left it. The Associated Press count in its latest state shows the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 176,162 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 173,649—a margin of 2,513 votes, with 92.64 percent of precincts reporting. Decision Desk HQ’s district file, timed November 5 at 1:21 a.m. EST, carries the same two totals, with the Libertarian, Douglas Mangeris, at 11,669 votes and 91 percent of the expected vote reported. About 30,000 ballots were reported outstanding in the district, concentrated in Douglas and Larimer counties. Colorado’s deadline for military and overseas ballots to arrive, and for voters to cure a missing or mismatched signature, is November 12. Colorado’s 3rd District remains uncalled, its leader disputed between two files the overnight edition printed; no newer count on the shelf this morning settles it.

Kansas’s governorship also stands where it stood. The Associated Press Kansas file shows the Democrat, Cindy Holscher, at 549,974 votes and the Republican, Ty Masterson, at 542,929—a margin of 7,045, with all precincts reporting, the race still too early to call. Decision Desk HQ’s Kansas file, timed November 5 at 9:14 a.m. EST, carries the identical totals. The secretary of state, Scott Schwab, has ordered close-race audits in six races that finished within one percent, the governorship among them, each a hand count of ballots in 10 percent of precincts. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day and received by Friday will be added. Holscher has declared victory; Masterson has not conceded; the governor, Laura Kelly, has congratulated Holscher as governor-elect. The statements stand, and the count proceeds underneath them.

The Markets’ Second Reading

Wednesday’s verdict is settled because Wednesday’s markets are closed: the Dow up 1,569.40 points, 3.03 percent, at 53,356.12; the S&P 500 up 1.58 percent at 7,688.62; the Nasdaq Composite up 1.44 percent at 25,736.51; Brent settled at $94.62, down 8.67 percent. The reasons traders gave were the ones the midnight edition recorded: the election ended the uncertainty, the president accepted the result, and oil fell on the expectation—an expectation, not an agreement—that the war with Iran will end sooner.

Thursday opened divided, on the same split Asia had shown overnight: the broad market held, the chip and data-center trade fell. Before the bell, Reuters’ futures file had Dow contracts up 258 points, or 0.48 percent, S&P 500 contracts up 0.5 points, and Nasdaq 100 contracts down 181 points, or 0.63 percent, at 5:04 a.m. ET. Qualcomm fell 10.1 percent in premarket trading after its fourth-quarter smartphone chip sales came in below estimates; Nvidia, Marvell, and Intel were down; the data-center operators and server makers were down; Amazon, Meta, and Alphabet were up about 0.5 percent each. A UBS note carried in the same file puts the question in figures: data-center pauses will slow the buildout into 2028, with about 30 percent of expected 2028 additions now at risk. At the opening bell the split held: Reuters’ opening report had the Dow up 330.63 points, or 0.62 percent, at 53,686.75, the S&P 500 down 12.86 points, or 0.17 percent, at 7,675.76, and the Nasdaq Composite down 198.95 points, or 0.77 percent, at 25,537.57. The live file’s 10:42 a.m. entry records the same pressure in two names: CoreWeave down 3 percent and Nebius down 6 percent on the day at that hour.

About an hour into the session the division became a general fall, and the desk prints the two states of the morning side by side because they do not reconcile into one. The early-session wrap, in quotes timed 15:41 GMT—10:41 a.m. ET—has all five of its tracked indexes lower: the Dow at 52,465.72, down 1.67 percent; the S&P 500 at 7,481.27, down 2.70 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,658.53, down 4.19 percent; the Nasdaq 100 down 4.79 percent; and the Russell 2000 down 2.00 percent. Inside the S&P 500, information technology fell furthest, down 5.31 percent, while consumer staples led with a gain of 1.29 percent—a rotation out of technology and into defensive shares, which the wrap, citing CNBC, attributes to concern that a Democratic Congress will bring more regulation of the artificial intelligence buildout. The figures are snapshots, not closes, and the wrap says so itself. Between the opening bell and 10:41 the Dow moved from up 0.62 percent to down 1.67 percent on the figures on the shelf; what the close will show belongs to the evening edition. Ahead of the market sit three Federal Reserve officials scheduled to speak during the day, Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin among them, and the October employment report on Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET.

Oil took back part of Wednesday’s fall, on the same reasoning in reverse. Reuters’ London file had Brent crude futures up about 2.5 percent at $96.8 a barrel, having fallen below $100 for the first time in two months in the overnight drop, and last up 2.5 percent at $97 in its later state; an earlier Reuters state of the same session had Brent up 78 cents, or 0.8 percent, at $95.40 as of 0900 GMT, with West Texas Intermediate up 11 cents at $88.23. The explanation the analysts quoted give is uncertainty, stated plainly by a UBS analyst in the file: the situation in the Middle East is still unresolved, and that is why there is some modest recovery in prices. The ten-year Treasury yield was unchanged on the day at 4.89 percent in the London file, the dollar had recovered part of its fall, and gold traded above $4,100 an ounce, up 5 percent in two days. Europe’s STOXX 600 rose another 0.4 percent, with bank shares up and semiconductor-exposed shares down.

London supplied the morning’s one completed official act in the markets’ column. Reuters’ report of the Bank of England’s decision records that the Monetary Policy Committee voted 8–1 to raise Bank Rate to 4 percent from 3.75 percent, and that the bank warned at least one more increase was likely if the conflict between the United States and Iran continues. The dissent ran toward a larger rise, not a hold: Catherine Mann voted for a half-point increase to 4.25 percent, saying she was concerned about non-linear inflation risks after consumer price inflation rose to 3.5 percent in September. The bank expects inflation to reach about 5 percent in the middle of next year and does not see it returning to the 2 percent target until the third quarter of 2028. Governor Andrew Bailey’s sentence is printed as he said it: “Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase.” The committee’s next decision is due December 17. The American election is two days old; its war is in a British central bank’s rate decision, in writing, at noon.

The Official Statements

The president’s position at noon is the one he stated at the ballroom, and a second account adds the name he gave it. Reuters’ Washington file of November 5 records the appearance: the president called reporters in to show the under-construction White House ballroom, said of the work, “For me, it’s relaxing,” and turned to the election briefly—“I’ll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto.” An account of his remarks to the New York Post carries the fuller version: “I guess I’ll become Mr. Veto. I’m not going to let them ruin it. And then at some point, we’ll probably make deals.” In the same account he said the Democrats did a good job and fought hard. The live file states the constitutional arithmetic beside the pledge: a veto can be overridden by two-thirds of both chambers, a threshold no count on the shelf gives either party. The president has said he will accept the results and work with the Democrats; he has also said what he will do with their bills. Both statements stand.

The incoming majority’s statements at noon describe a program and a first target. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become the first Black Speaker of the House, told reporters the incoming majority would be focused on affordability and accountability: “We don’t work for Donald Trump. We work for the American people. And the days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over.” An account of the party’s legislative planning records what the majority says it will move first when the new Congress convenes in January: repeal of the president’s tariff measures, legislation strengthening congressional authority over tariff decisions, and a requirement of congressional approval to continue the war with Iran. Jeffries, in a television interview carried in the same account, put the order of business as he sees it: “The American people do not want us to seek revenge. They want us to deliver results on their behalf because the cost of living is too high.” On the trade file specifically, the account of the trade agenda records Representative Richard Neal, expected to return to the chairmanship of the Ways and Means Committee: “We know they are tired of paying for Trump’s needless war with Iran and price-hiking tariffs every time they visit the checkout counter or the gas pump.” The same account states the limit: the majority can pass the bills and hold the hearings, and the veto stands at the end of both.

The Republican accounting continued in the morning, in the party’s own words, and two of its senators named the same two causes. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, in a social media post carried in the live file’s 10:23 a.m. entry, called the result a “blue tsunami” and used a plainer phrase beside it, and wrote: “Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high. Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long.” Cruz noted that Texans had not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994 and swept the posts on Tuesday. Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska, who is retiring, stated the party’s choice in one sentence: “If we don’t change, we’ll take more beatings.” The vice president’s post of the night before stands unretracted at noon—“The reason we lost is the war”—with the president’s answer beside it, that the war drove gasoline up a little bit in the short term and that he would do it again because Iran cannot be allowed a nuclear weapon. Speaker Mike Johnson’s announcement that he will not seek the leadership of the Republican minority in January also stands. On the other side of the Capitol’s new arithmetic, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan spent part of the morning stating, on two programs carried in the live file, that he will work with Republicans who said the harshest things about him during the campaign, naming Senator Cruz and a condition: good faith. His sentence on the vice president’s part in January is the morning’s lightest entry and is printed as he said it: constitutionally, the vice president is obligated to swear him in.

The Strait at Noon

No agreement was announced in the morning, and the state of the talks at noon is the state the overnight edition left, with one clarification added. The account of the mediation filed below records that Qatar has intensified its efforts, that both governments are reviewing the proposals the mediators have submitted, and that a senior Iranian official’s statement stands: the two sides remain a considerable distance from a deal, and Tehran’s conditions—removal of oil sanctions, an end to the American naval blockade, and the release of frozen assets—must be met before the Strait of Hormuz reopens. The clarification concerns the clock: an official familiar with the discussions said responses from the two capitals were expected within 36 hours, and the senior Iranian official later stated there was no fixed deadline for exchanging messages through the mediators or reviewing the proposals. Iran’s stated basis remains its seven-step plan of September, which Tehran says can now be implemented within two days of acceptance, the strait reopening inside that window. From Washington there is no agreement and no new word on the draft. Oil rose in the morning on the absence of an agreement; that is a fact about the market’s reading, recorded in the markets’ section above, and it is the only movement the strait produced by noon.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the House: 233 called seats in Ballotpedia’s Thursday accounting with 64 races open, 235 won and 26 led in the Associated Press tracker carried overnight, 242 called in NBC’s Wednesday-evening count, and 251 called in Decision Desk HQ’s own totals with 31 open—four call desks, four hours, one chamber, and a final Democratic total estimated between 249 and 268 by the offices that estimate such things. Second, Mississippi: the same race at 1,138 votes in the wire figures, 1,720 in a tally updated at 10:14 this morning, and 1,852 and 1,818 in two states of the Decision Desk count—the leader identical in every bearing, the margin a range, and the ballots that will settle it dated November 10 and November 13. Third, the market: the Dow up 0.62 percent at the opening bell in the wire’s report and down 1.67 percent at 10:41 in the early-session wrap, the Nasdaq down 0.77 percent at the open and down 4.19 percent an hour later—a disagreement that may be nothing but the record of a market turning inside a single morning, printed because a reader checking either file against this page will find the other number. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the midday are single-valued: no race was called in the morning; Alaska stands at 637 votes and November 18; Colorado’s 4th stands at 2,513; Kansas stands at 7,045 with its audit ordered; Brent is back above $95 after settling at $94.62; the Bank of England raised its rate to 4 percent by 8–1 with the dissent asking for more; and the president’s word for his next two years, in his own coinage, is Mr. Veto. The count belongs to the clerks until Friday’s mail arrives in Mississippi and Kansas. The session belongs to the close. The log proceeds to the evening.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-three items.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska and Mississippi both too early to call, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
The Business Standard — why Alaska and Mississippi have not been called

Mississippi’s 1,138-vote margin, its November 10 and November 13 dates, no runoff in the procedure, and no automatic recount; Alaska’s mail windows and its November 18 ranked-choice tabulation.

Subjective
Votendi, carrying Decision Desk HQ — the live results file

The November 5 update: 251 House seats called for Democrats and 153 for Republicans with 31 uncalled; Mississippi at 466,464 to 464,612 in a source update of November 4, 6:38 p.m. EST, and at 466,689 to 464,871 in its later state panel; Alaska at 102,962 to 102,325. A lead is never treated as a race call.

Subjective
Poliwave — the Senate live map

Updated November 5 at 10:14 a.m. EST: 33 of 35 Senate races called, Alaska and Mississippi counting; Mississippi at 466,246 to 464,526; Alaska at 102,962 to 102,325.

Subjective
Ballotpedia News — the Thursday accounting

At least 30 House districts gained and a 233–138 called majority, with 64 races uncalled; projections of 249 and 255 carried; the Senate’s swing meeting its wave threshold and the House’s not yet; 21 Democratic trifectas, the most since 1992.

Subjective
Kacee Allen Network — both chambers in January

Democrats to organize both chambers, checked against CBS News and Reuters on the morning of November 5: a final House estimate of 251 to 268, Jeffries expecting at least 255, and Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled.

Subjective
Associated Press — Colorado’s 4th District

Laubacher 176,162, Boebert 173,649, with 92.64 percent of precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Decision Desk HQ — Colorado’s 4th District

Timed November 5 at 1:21 a.m. EST: Laubacher 176,162, or 48.73 percent; Boebert 173,649, or 48.04 percent; Mangeris 11,669; 91 percent of the expected vote reported, and the race not called.

Subjective
Associated Press — Governor, Kansas

Holscher 549,974, Masterson 542,929, with all precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Decision Desk HQ — Governor, Kansas

Timed November 5 at 9:14 a.m. EST: Holscher 549,974, or 50.32 percent; Masterson 542,929, or 49.68 percent; more than 95 percent of the vote reported.

Subjective
Reuters — futures steady, Nasdaq lags

At 5:04 a.m. ET: Dow contracts up 0.48 percent, S&P 500 contracts up 0.01 percent, Nasdaq 100 contracts down 0.63 percent; Qualcomm down 10.1 percent premarket; the UBS note putting about 30 percent of expected 2028 data-center additions at risk; three Fed officials to speak, and Friday’s October jobs report ahead.

Subjective
Reuters, via WTBX — the opening bell

The Nasdaq opened lower as chip and data-center stocks fell and broader markets were muted: the Dow up 330.63 points, or 0.62 percent, at 53,686.75; the S&P 500 down 0.17 percent at 7,675.76; the Nasdaq Composite down 0.77 percent at 25,537.57.

Subjective
The Edge — the early-session wrap, November 5

Quotes timed 15:41 GMT, about an hour into the session: all five tracked indexes lower, the S&P 500 down 2.70 percent and the Nasdaq 100 down 4.79 percent; information technology down 5.31 percent and consumer staples up 1.29 percent inside the S&P 500; CNBC’s rotation account cited; the snapshots stated not to be closes.

Subjective
TipRanks — futures mixed, November 5

At 5:25 a.m. EST: Nasdaq 100 futures down 0.53 percent, S&P 500 futures up 0.05 percent, Dow futures up 0.49 percent, after Wednesday’s session in which the Dow rose 3.03 percent, the S&P 500 1.58 percent, and the Nasdaq Composite 1.44 percent.

Subjective
Reuters, via Kitco — AI stocks fall, oil bounces back

Chip stocks down on concern about restraint on the AI buildout; Brent up about 2.5 percent at $96.8 and last at $97; the STOXX 600 up 0.4 percent; gold above $4,100, up 5 percent in two days; the ten-year yield unchanged at 4.89 percent; the euro at $1.1222 after the Bank of England’s decision.

Subjective
Reuters, via MyMixFM — oil rises as investors weigh the war

London, November 5: Brent up 78 cents, or 0.8 percent, at $95.40 as of 0900 GMT and West Texas Intermediate up 11 cents at $88.23, after both fell more than 8 percent in the previous session to their lowest settlements since August 31; the UBS analyst’s sentence that the Middle East situation is still unresolved.

Subjective
Reuters — the Bank of England raises rates

Bank Rate raised to 4 percent from 3.75 percent by 8–1, Catherine Mann voting for 4.25 percent; inflation expected to reach about 5 percent in the middle of next year and to return to target in the third quarter of 2028; Governor Bailey’s statement that the increase is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is resolved; the members’ differing views on further rises printed.

Subjective
Reuters, via HI-99 — Democrats vow to rein in the president

Washington, November 5: the incoming majority’s focus on affordability and accountability in Jeffries’s words; the president’s ballroom appearance and his veto sentence; the war acknowledged and stood by; the vice president’s post quoted; Governor DeSantis’s extinction-level description; Speaker Johnson’s decision not to lead his caucus next year; and the lame-duck funding measure ahead.

Subjective
USA Today — the live file, November 5

The running file of the second morning: Secretary Watson’s Mississippi statement at 7:06 a.m.; Alaska’s 637 votes at 6:51 a.m.; Senator Cruz’s cost-of-living post at 10:23 a.m.; Senator-elect El-Sayed’s interviews at 10:25 and 10:43 a.m.; Representative Bacon’s sentence; Chairman Martin’s statement; and data-center and AI stocks down at 10:42 a.m., CoreWeave down 3 percent and Nebius down 6 percent.

Subjective
Mandatory — “Mr. Veto”

The president’s remarks to the New York Post as reported: he will become “Mr. Veto,” will turn the Democrats down for a month or two, and expects deals after; the red VETO cap photograph; his Fox News remarks praising the Democrats’ campaign and faulting candidates who fought him.

Subjective
Aju Press — Jeffries and the legislative program

The incoming majority’s plans as reported: repeal of the tariff measures, congressional authority over tariff decisions, and congressional approval to continue the war with Iran; Jeffries’s interview statement that voters want results on the cost of living, not revenge; Representative Raskin’s statement on the tariffs; and the veto arithmetic stated.

Subjective
BusinessWorld — the trade agenda and the veto wall

Trade and legal experts on what the majority can and cannot do on tariffs: funding leverage and hearings on one side, the veto and the two-thirds override figures—67 senators and 290 House members—on the other; Representative Neal’s statement on costs, health care, and the war.

Subjective
AnewZ — tensions persist as Qatar pushes for a deal

Qatar’s mediation intensified; both governments reviewing the mediators’ proposals; the senior Iranian official’s statement that the sides remain far apart and that Tehran’s conditions must precede the strait’s reopening; the 36-hour expectation for responses, and the later statement that no fixed deadline exists.

entry.title: The Night the Count Stood Still
entry.summary: The overnight file for November 5, 2026: no new call in the night, Mississippi's ballot calendar stated plainly, Colorado's 4th narrows, Asia sells the chips again, oil tests $93, Qatar's mediators wait, and the vice president's full accounting. Collected at 0400.
entry.content:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The Night the Count Stood Still

At 0400 no new race had been called in the night. What the night produced instead was the calendar: the dates on which Mississippi and Alaska will finish, stated plainly; a narrower margin in Colorado’s 4th; a second Asian selling of the chip trade; oil testing $93; a draft agreement circulating in Doha with no signature on it; and the vice president’s full accounting of the defeat, printed where his party could read it.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Thursday, November 5, 2026. This edition continues the log of the midterm count from Edition No. 5, the Midnight Watch. Where the overnight reporting corrects a procedure this paper carried on Wednesday—Mississippi’s, below—the correction is printed in the open and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

No call moved in the night, in either chamber, in any state. The Senate stands where the midnight edition left it: 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled. The Associated Press House tracker in its latest state is also unchanged: 235 seats won by Democrats and 26 led, against 146 won and 28 led for Republicans, with 26 seats still too close to call. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats with Alaska and Kansas open. Control of no chamber and no majority is in question in any count on the shelf. The night’s work was not the result; it was the schedule on which the remainder of the result will arrive, and the readings that Asia, Tehran, and the Republican Party’s own vice president put on the result while Washington slept.

Two facts organize the night: the remaining counting is now dated—Mississippi certifies by November 13, Alaska tabulates on November 18—and the war is still unsettled, with a draft circulating in Doha, unverified claims of fresh tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, and oil priced as if the war were ending anyway.

Mississippi: The Calendar, Stated Plainly

The overnight explainer, carrying the Associated Press’s account, corrects the procedure this paper printed on Wednesday, and the correction is filed first. Mississippi does not require a majority in a regular federal general election. The candidate with the most votes wins; there is no runoff. The December 1 runoff date carried in Editions No. 2, 4, and 5 of this paper does not apply to this race, and the desk withdraws it here, in the next edition in the log, which is where a log corrects itself. The count itself stands as the midnight edition left it in its latest figure: the Democrat, Scott Colom, at 464,926 votes, 49 percent, and the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, at 463,788, 48.9 percent—a margin of 1,138 votes, with an estimated 96 percent of votes counted, per the account of why the two Senate races have not been called filed below. Al Jazeera’s account of the same delay carries the same margin and the same leader.

What remains, and by when: approximately 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots still to be received within five business days, and an unknown number of affidavit ballots, per the November 4 statement of Michael Watson, the secretary of state, quoted in both accounts. A voter who cast an affidavit ballot for lack of acceptable identification has until November 10 to present it. Counties have until November 13 to submit certified results. Mississippi holds no automatic recounts; a candidate seeking one would have to obtain a court order, per the Associated Press. The wire calls a race when the trailing candidate has no path left to close the gap; here the path runs through several thousand ballots against a margin of 1,138, and it stays open until they are counted.

Alaska: Eleven Days of Mail, Then the Tabulation

Alaska’s Senate count did not move in the night; its procedure is also now fully stated. The Associated Press Senate file still shows 75.43 percent of precincts reporting, and the Democrat, Mary Peltola, still leads the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan—by 626 votes in the Associated Press figures carried in the overnight explainer, and by 637 in the same wire’s evening dashboard entry carried in the midnight edition. The desk prints both numbers; they are two states of one unfinished count. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holds 3,583 votes, more than either margin. Alaska accepts domestic mail ballots for up to 10 days after Election Day and overseas ballots for up to 15 days, provided they were mailed by November 3. If no candidate clears 50 percent of first choices—both leaders are below it—the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18.

The legal file around the count, stated without weight on either side: the Justice Department sued to block certification if the incumbent loses; Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit on November 1, ruling that the government had offered no workable plan to investigate ballots cast for the second Sullivan while preserving ballot secrecy; the department has said it will appeal. The governor, Mike Dunleavy, has ordered a state investigation and has suggested he may not certify a Peltola victory, per the Associated Press account filed below. Peltola has said her campaign had no involvement in the second Sullivan’s candidacy, and he has said he had no contact with her campaign about running. Each statement stands as its maker made it. In the governorship, the Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, holds 49.2 percent of first choices with about 74 percent counted, the Republican Bernadette Wilson second at about 29 percent—the same November 18 schedule if no majority emerges.

Colorado and Kansas: The Counts That Moved

Colorado’s 4th District narrowed in the night, toward the incumbent. The Associated Press count in its latest state shows the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 176,162 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 173,649—a margin of 2,513 votes, with 92.64 percent of precincts reporting. The midnight edition carried the same file at 174,963 to 171,711, a margin of 3,252. The race remains too early to call. The account of the incumbent’s path filed below puts about 30,000 ballots outstanding, concentrated in Douglas and Larimer counties, and records her own figure from Wednesday evening: “We’re about a 5,000-vote deficit right now, a little bit less than that.” Colorado’s deadline for military and overseas ballots to arrive, and for voters to cure a missing or mismatched signature, is November 12.

Colorado’s 3rd District is reported two ways, and the desk prints both. The midnight edition, following the Colorado live file as it signed off for the night, carried the Democrat, Dwayne Romero, leading the Republican incumbent, Jeff Hurd, by more than 2,200 votes with 88 percent counted. The Rocky Mountain Voice file, in an update timed 8:22 a.m. Wednesday, reports Hurd ahead by 1,211 votes. The two files cannot both describe the same state of the count; they were taken at different hours from different tallies, and the race is uncalled in both. Which man leads the 3rd District at 0400 is a question the next counts will answer, and it is filed here as open.

Kansas’s governorship did not move in the night, and its audit is now general. The Associated Press Kansas file stands at 549,974 votes for the Democrat, Cindy Holscher, and 542,929 for the Republican, Ty Masterson—a margin of 7,045, with all precincts reporting, the race still too early to call. The secretary of state, Scott Schwab, has ordered close-race audits in six races that finished within one percent—governor, secretary of state, attorney general, and three state House districts—each a hand count of ballots in 10 percent of precincts, per the account of the audits filed below. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day and received by Friday will be added. Holscher has declared victory; Masterson has not conceded; the governor, Laura Kelly, has congratulated Holscher as governor-elect. All three statements stand, and the count proceeds underneath them.

Asia: The Second Selling of the AI Trade

Asia’s Thursday session repeated Wednesday’s pattern in sharper form: the chip trade sold, and nearly everything else rose. Reuters’ Singapore file reports oil, chip stocks, and the dollar under pressure and broad indexes higher, on the same reasoning the American session used: a clear electoral outcome, and the expectation—an expectation, not an agreement—that the war with Iran will end sooner under a Democratic Congress. Brent crude futures fell nearly 9 percent overnight, below $100 a barrel, and stand about 20 percent lower on the week; if the fall holds through Friday’s close it is the largest weekly drop since April 2020, when American crude briefly traded below zero. In the Asia morning Brent was testing its lows at $93.50; a Dow Jones account carried front-month Brent at $93.85, down 0.8 percent on the day in Asia, and West Texas Intermediate at $86.93, down 1.4 percent. The dollar fell to a one-month low of $1.1273 per euro. The ten-year Treasury yield fell 6 basis points overnight and a further point in early Tokyo trade, to 4.87 percent.

The selling sat in the same names, and the percentages differ by the hour each file was taken. Reuters’ morning figures: the KOSPI down 4 percent and near a seven-month low, Taiwan down 1.8 percent, the Nikkei down 0.5 percent. The Asia-Pacific market file filed below, taken later in the session, carries the KOSPI down about 4.8 percent after a sidecar—a five-minute halt to program trading—was triggered, the Nikkei down about 1.5 percent while the broader Topix rose about 1.4 percent, Shanghai up about 3.6 percent, and the Hang Seng up about 3 percent. SoftBank fell about 5.8 percent, on the slide in its chip designer Arm and a Financial Times report that Chinese regulators will not allow its $5.4 billion acquisition of ABB’s robotics division. Solar shares rose the most in the Reuters account; data-centre companies and their suppliers fell across Asia. In India, the Nifty 50 rose more than 2 percent to 24,442.20 and the Sensex more than 2 percent to 79,001.19, on the fall in crude. Gold extended Wednesday’s rise of about 3 percent to about $4,135 an ounce. A Melbourne strategist quoted by Reuters states the markets’ position in one sentence: “The magnitude of the victory is what has caught markets off guard.”

The Strait and the Draft

No agreement was announced in the night, and the two public accounts of the talks do not describe the same distance. On one bearing, a draft is close: reports carried in the Indian market coverage state that the United States has approved a draft understanding passed to Iran through Qatari mediators, and the account of the Qatar-presented draft filed below reports that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were briefed and approved it, that concessions cover Iran’s nuclear program and its frozen assets, and that the timing of simultaneous announcements is under discussion. On the other bearing, the distance stands: a senior Iranian official told Reuters the two sides remain far from a deal, that Tehran’s conditions must be met if the United States wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened, and that feedback on the mediators’ latest suggestion was expected from both capitals within 36 hours; the Qatari team has returned to Doha and the talks continue through the mediators, per the Reuters account of the diplomatic push filed below. Iran’s stated basis remains its seven-step plan of September: an end to the American naval blockade, a waiver on oil sales and cancellation of new sanctions, reopening of the strait—which Tehran says it can now do within two days of an agreement—and talks on the remaining issues, including the nuclear program, to follow. The secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, has said the American reply was not convincing and all seven conditions must be answered clearly. From Washington there is no agreement and one sentence of posture: the president has said the United States has no immediate plans for military action.

Two further facts stand beside the talks, each attributed. First, Tehran is on high alert: two senior Iranian sources told Reuters that while Iranian leaders welcomed the Democrats’ victory, they were concerned the president could seek to compensate for it with a military strike, per Reuters’ account of the Iranian response filed below. Second, the strait itself produced claims in the night that the desk cannot verify and prints as claims: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in the strait and that a tanker using an unapproved route had struck a mine, per the Asia-Pacific market file; a separate report carried the Guards’ navy saying three oil tankers hit mines on Tuesday. No second source on the shelf confirms either incident. Oil fell through both claims, which is a fact about the market’s reading, not about the strait.

The Vice President’s Accounting

The fullest Republican document of the night is the vice president’s, and it was published where his own party reads. Le Monde’s overnight analysis carries the post in substance. JD Vance wrote: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.” And: “To the people who are pissed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so.” The post’s analysis of the vote is that the loss was not a turnout failure: many people who voted for the Trump–Vance ticket in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. Its four lessons are ending the war in Iran, focusing on the cost of living, adhering to the America First doctrine, and reassessing the relationship with Israel. On immigration enforcement, the vice president wrote that he is open to changing the approach, for instance by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor.

The rest of the party’s argument ran in the same hours, in the open. The president, asked at the White House ballroom construction site about the vice president’s assessment, answered: “Well, I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term, and probably that’s true, but at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because, long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, who leaves office in January, described the midterms as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans.” The commentator Rod Dreher, long close to the vice president, wrote that the president should resign and let the vice president run things for the next two years, and called him a spent force; the commentator Matt Walsh called him, on Tuesday evening, “yesterday’s news.” The Speaker, Mike Johnson, announced Wednesday morning he will not seek the leadership of the Republican minority in January. Former Ambassador Nikki Haley stated the contrary lesson: “When we stay close to our policies, we win: economic freedom, lower taxes, smaller government, making sure we get families back to work, national security.” Nothing in the argument was settled overnight; the 2028 succession is now an open question inside a party that still holds the White House, the veto, and the command of the armed forces.

The World’s Morning Papers

Europe’s second-day readings divide between welcome, caution, and the judgment that nothing structural has changed. The roundup of the world leaders’ reactions filed below carries them in sequence. Germany’s defense minister, Boris Pistorius, congratulated the Democrats on a historic victory and stated that Europe must continue assuming greater responsibility for its own security. France’s economy and finance minister, Roland Lescure, called the gains undeniable and cautioned that the president retains significant authority over American foreign policy. Italy’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, said the results would not alter relations between Rome and Washington. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, welcomed the victory as a positive development for American democracy; the Czech prime minister, Andrej Babiš, called it expected but exceptionally large. The co-leader of Germany’s AfD, Alice Weidel, stated the reading from the other side of her country’s politics: the president had promised his voters no interventionist foreign policy, and the broken promise had come back to haunt the Republicans. Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, stated the cost-of-living reading in general form: “The world now has an opportunity to unite around an issue that affects us all, and that’s the cost of living.” Belgium’s defense minister, Theo Franken, stated the governing reading: with so many internal divisions, it will be nearly impossible to govern in the United States over the next few years.

The other capitals held the positions the earlier watches recorded. China’s foreign ministry spokeswoman, Mao Ning, described the election as a domestic matter that will not change Beijing’s position. The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, expressed hope that the president would continue pursuing diplomatic solutions; the deputy foreign minister, Sergei Ryabkov, counseled waiting for the final results. In Tehran, the newspaper Hamshahri printed the anniversary of the 1979 embassy seizure beside the election under the headline “Iran’s shadow over US elections,” with an image of the president blindfolded and his head bowed. In London, the Guardian’s readers divided between enthusiasm and the repeated caution that Washington may return to business as usual. Each capital’s reading is printed as that capital made it; the disagreement is itself the record of the night abroad.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Colorado’s 3rd District: one Colorado file carries the Democrat ahead by more than 2,200 votes as its night closed, another carries the Republican ahead by 1,211 in a Wednesday-morning update—the leader itself in dispute until the next counts. Second, the Asian percentages: the KOSPI down 4 percent in the morning file and about 4.8 percent in the later one, the Nikkei down 0.5 and about 1.5, Brent at $93.50, $93.85, and about $97 in three files taken at different hours of one falling market—a disagreement of clocks, printed because a reader checking any one file against this page will find the other numbers. Third, the talks in Doha: one set of reports has a draft approved in Washington and welcomed in two Gulf capitals, and the named Iranian officials on the record say the American reply is unconvincing and the two sides far apart. Both bearings are printed above; an agreement exists when both capitals announce one, and neither has. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the night are single-valued: no race was called; Mississippi’s calendar runs to November 10 and 13 with no runoff in the procedure; Alaska’s runs to November 18; Colorado’s 4th narrowed to 2,513 votes; oil fell below $100 and tested $93; and the vice president’s sentence—“The reason we lost is the war”—stands unretracted, with the president’s answer beside it. The log proceeds on the clerks’ schedules now, not on Washington’s. The next count belongs to the states.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-four items.

Subjective
The Business Standard — why Alaska and Mississippi have not been called

The Associated Press had not called either Senate race by Thursday. Mississippi: Colom leads Hyde-Smith by 1,138 votes, about 3,600 mail ballots outstanding, affidavit identification due by November 10, counties to certify by November 13, the most votes wins with no runoff, and no automatic recount. Alaska: Peltola leads Sullivan by 626 votes, mail accepted for 10 days domestic and 15 overseas, ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18, the certification suit dismissed November 1 with an appeal stated, and the governor’s race on the same schedule.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the two Senate calls

Colom ahead by 1,138 votes on Wednesday night with about 96 percent counted and a few thousand provisional and mail ballots left; Peltola ahead by 637 with nearly a quarter of Alaska’s votes uncounted; Mississippi’s 10 days to process and five business days for mail; Alaska’s ranked-choice results to be published November 18.

Subjective
Agence France-Presse, via Ekkow — Mississippi cliffhanger, Alaska count continues

The two uncalled Senate races on Wednesday: Colom ahead by less than 50 votes in the CNN and NBC counts the story cites, with thousands of eligibility-check ballots uncounted; Peltola at 48.2 percent to Sullivan’s 47.9 with 74 percent counted; the second Sullivan at 3,583 votes, more than the 626 separating the front-runners; and a result that may not be declared for weeks.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska too early to call at 75.43 percent of precincts reporting, Mississippi too early to call at 99.83 percent, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
Associated Press — House balance of power

235 House seats won by Democrats and 26 more led, against 146 won and 28 led for Republicans, in the tracker’s latest state—unchanged overnight.

Subjective
Associated Press — Colorado’s 4th District

Laubacher 176,162, Boebert 173,649, with 92.64 percent of precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Times Now World — Boebert trails in Colorado

The incumbent’s path described as increasingly difficult, with about 30,000 ballots outstanding in Douglas and Larimer counties, the shares she would need in each to close the gap, and her Wednesday-evening statement: “We’re about a 5,000-vote deficit right now, a little bit less than that.”

Subjective
Rocky Mountain Voice — Colorado’s federal races

The state file with its Wednesday update: Hurd pulled ahead of Romero in the 3rd District by 1,211 votes as of 8:22 a.m.; the 3rd, 4th, and 5th districts uncalled; the 8th settled for the Democrats; Douglas County’s count in the 4th, where Laubacher leads with half the district’s registration; and November 12 as the deadline for overseas ballots and signature cures.

Subjective
Associated Press — Governor, Kansas

Holscher 549,974, Masterson 542,929, with all precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Johnson County Post — Kansas orders audits in six close races

Six races within one percent to be audited by hand count in 10 percent of precincts: governor, secretary of state, attorney general, and House Districts 27, 40, and 117. Holscher’s victory statement, Masterson’s answer that the margin calls for another look, and the sitting governor’s congratulations to the governor-elect are printed in the same story.

Subjective
State Capital Lobbyist — where things stand, Wednesday evening

The standing accounting the night began from: the Senate at 54 to 44 with two uncalled, 26 House seats open, 28 governorships held by the Democrats, and at least nine legislative chambers flipped, every one in the same direction.

Subjective
Reuters — oil and data centre stocks sink in Asia

Filed from Singapore for Thursday: Brent down nearly 9 percent overnight and about 20 percent on the week, testing $93.50; the dollar at a one-month low of $1.1273 per euro; the ten-year yield at 4.87 percent in early Tokyo trade; the KOSPI down 4 percent, Taiwan down 1.8 percent, the Nikkei down 0.5 percent; solar shares up the most; and the Melbourne strategist’s sentence on the magnitude of the victory catching markets off guard.

Subjective
Dow Jones Newswires, via Morningstar — oil extends decline, Asian stocks mixed

Thursday, 01:02 ET: oil extending its decline into the Asian session, front-month West Texas Intermediate down 1.4 percent at $86.93 and Brent down 0.8 percent at $93.85; Asian stocks mixed on brighter prospects for Middle East peace and a cloudier outlook for AI spending; the 10-year Japanese government bond yield down 5.8 basis points to 2.76 percent; and the president’s Wall Street Journal acknowledgment that the war contributed to the losses, without regret.

Subjective
investingLive — Asia-Pacific market news, Thursday

The later state of the Asian session: the KOSPI down about 4.8 percent after a sidecar halted program trading, the Nikkei down about 1.5 percent while the Topix rose about 1.4 percent, Shanghai up about 3.6 percent and the Hang Seng about 3 percent, SoftBank down about 5.8 percent with the report of China blocking its ABB robotics acquisition, Brent around $97 and West Texas Intermediate around $88 in its figures, gold at about $4,135, and the Revolutionary Guards’ claims of tanker fires and a mine strike in the strait, noted as unverified.

Subjective
Devdiscourse — chip stocks, oil sink in the aftermath

The Reuters markets file in a second carrying: the KOSPI down nearly 6 percent in its figures, Taiwan down over 3 percent and poised for its worst week since April 2025, European futures up 0.2 percent, Nasdaq futures down 1 percent, Brent at $94.21 testing overnight lows, and the ten-year yield at 4.85 percent in its last state.

Subjective
Outlook Business — Nifty surges as crude falls

Thursday in Mumbai: the Nifty 50 up more than 2 percent to 24,442.20 and the Sensex up more than 2 percent to 79,001.19, on Brent below $95 and expectations of diplomatic progress in the war; the report that the United States has approved a draft understanding passed to Iran through Qatari mediators, credited with pulling the war premium out of crude; and the strait’s share of world petroleum trade stated at 20 to 25 percent.

Subjective
Reuters — Indian shares set to open higher

GIFT Nifty futures at 24,295.5 on Thursday morning against a Wednesday close of 23,960.6; Brent down 1 percent to $93.50 after the previous session’s 8.7 percent slide; the Democratic win read as a rebuke to the president, with the tariff policy and the war named among the causes of the Indian market’s underperformance this year.

Subjective
Le Monde — the vice president’s post, and the party’s argument

The November 5 analysis: the vice president’s full post, with the war at its center, the four lessons, the 2024 voters who changed sides, and the enforcement change he is open to; the president’s answer at the ballroom site; Governor DeSantis’s extinction-level description; the commentator Dreher’s resignation call; Ambassador Haley’s contrary lesson; and Speaker Johnson’s decision not to seek the minority leadership.

Subjective
Reuters — Iranian officials on the vote

The parliament speaker’s “Americans said NO TO WAR” and the supreme leader’s written statement that American hostility persists regardless of party, printed with the two senior sources’ account that Tehran welcomed the result and remains on high alert against a compensating strike, the mediators’ intensified efforts, and the Hamshahri front page: “Iran’s shadow over US elections.”

Subjective
Al Jazeera — the supreme leader’s warning, and the speaker’s message

Anyone expecting a shift in American policy toward Iran is “seriously mistaken,” in the supreme leader’s written statement, with a wider response warned if attacks resume; the parliament speaker’s “NO TO WAR” endorsement and nightmare warning printed beside it; and the president’s distinction that it was the gasoline prices, not the war.

Subjective
Reuters, via i3investor — deal still out of reach, Qatar pushes

A senior Iranian official’s account: the two sides still far from a deal, mediators working hard to narrow gaps, the Qatari team returned to Doha with talks continuing, feedback expected from both capitals within 36 hours, and Tehran’s conditions required before the strait reopens.

Subjective
Daily The Destination — the Qatar-presented draft

Sources’ account that the United States approved the Qatar-presented draft memorandum, that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were briefed and approved it, that concessions cover the nuclear program and frozen assets with simultaneous announcements under discussion—and the security council secretary’s answer that the American reply to Iran’s seven conditions was not convincing.

Subjective
EuropeSays — world leaders offer mixed reactions

The leaders in sequence: Pistorius’s congratulations with Europe’s own security responsibility; Weidel on the broken non-intervention promise; Sánchez’s rejection reading; Lescure’s undeniable gains with the president’s foreign-policy authority retained; Tajani’s unchanged relations; Tusk’s welcome; Babiš’s expected but exceptionally large; Schaldemose’s cautious optimism for Ukraine; Mao Ning’s domestic matter; Peskov’s hope for diplomatic solutions; and Ryabkov’s counsel to wait.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — international politicians react

The collected statements as filed: Spain’s and Norway’s prime ministers, South Africa’s president’s new era in world relations, the European Parliament vice president’s cautious optimism, the Greek spokesman’s strong relations, Russia’s deputy foreign minister quoted by RIA, Japan’s chief cabinet secretary, France’s finance minister, and Germany’s parties from both directions.

entry.title: What the Day Settled, What It Left Open
entry.summary: The midnight file for November 5, 2026: at 0000 control of Congress, the governors' majority, nine statehouse chambers, and the market close are settled; Alaska, Mississippi, Kansas, Colorado, and 26 House seats are left open, with the war, the veto, and impeachment unanswered. Edition No. 5, the Midnight Watch.
entry.content:
The Midterm Elections — The Last Entry of the Day

Objective

What the Day Settled, What It Left Open

At 0000 the day’s work can be divided cleanly. Settled: control of both chambers of Congress, a majority of the governorships, at least nine state legislative chambers, and the closing prices of the markets. Left open: two Senate seats, two governorships, 26 House seats, and every question that begins on January 3.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Thursday, November 5, 2026—the midnight that begins this date and closes the day before it. This edition completes the log of November 4 begun in Edition No. 3, the Overnight Watch, continued in Edition No. 2, the Midday Watch, and carried whole in Edition No. 4, the Evening Watch. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight count differs from the evening count, the difference is stated here, in the open.

What the Day Settled

Congress is settled, and was settled before the day began. Democrats hold the Senate, 54 seats to the Republicans’ 44, with two races uncalled. The seven flipped seats stand and none flipped the other way: Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, and Maine. Senate control was called at 11:39 p.m. Tuesday on the Iowa result, per the evening accounting of where things stand, filed below. In the House, the Associated Press tracker in its latest state shows 235 seats won by Democrats and 26 more led, against 146 won and 28 led for Republicans—up from the evening state of 232 won and 29 led. Control is not in question in any count on the shelf. What the counts still argue about is arithmetic, and the cocked hat below prints it.

The governors’ majority is settled. Democrats hold 28 of the 50 governorships, a majority for the first time in 16 years, with five offices changed in party—Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Nevada, the last called during the afternoon. Two races remain open, in Alaska and Kansas, and neither can change the majority. Below Washington, the statehouse result is also settled in its direction: at least nine state legislative chambers changed hands, every one of them to the Democrats—the Pennsylvania Senate, both Wisconsin chambers, the North Carolina House, both New Hampshire chambers, the Minnesota House, which had been tied, and, by Wednesday afternoon, the Michigan House and the Texas House. The National Conference of State Legislatures’ accounting lists the same chambers, and Reuters’ state-level report records the trifectas gained in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin and the Republican trifectas broken in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas. No chamber flipped to the Republicans.

The markets’ verdict is settled because the markets are closed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,569.40 points, 3.03 percent, at 53,356.12—its strongest post-midterm performance in 44 years, per the closing accounts. The S&P 500 closed up 1.58 percent at 7,688.62 and the Nasdaq Composite up 1.44 percent at 25,736.51. Oil finished what it began at midday: Brent settled at $94.62 a barrel, down $8.98, or 8.67 percent, and West Texas Intermediate settled at $88.12, down $7.97, or 8.29 percent, per the settlement figures carried in the closing report filed below. The fear gauge settled with them: the VIX closed at 16.61, down 20.26 percent, and the ten-year Treasury yield ended the day at 4.888 percent, below 5 percent. Gold rose about 3.3 percent to about $4,070 an ounce. In the evening futures trade the verdict simply held: Dow futures up 0.14 percent, S&P 500 futures up 0.11 percent, Nasdaq futures up 0.02 percent, per the after-close report. The reasons traders gave are the same at midnight as at the close: the election ended the uncertainty, the president accepted the result, and oil fell on the expectation—an expectation, not an agreement—that the war with Iran will end sooner than it would have on Tuesday morning.

The Count That Did Not Finish

Mississippi moved during the evening, toward the challenger, and stayed uncalled. The USA Today live file, in its 8:00 p.m. ET entry, put the Democrat, Scott Colom, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 1,138 votes, with about 96 percent of ballots counted, on the Associated Press dashboard. The evening edition of this paper carried the wire’s table at a margin of 65 votes; the noon edition carried counts of 43 and 2,169 from other tallies. The leader has not changed in any count all day. The margin has been reported at four figures, and the desk prints the latest and the range together in the cocked hat. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day are still arriving, affidavit ballots are still being processed, and if neither candidate clears 50 percent the seat is decided in a runoff on December 1. The account of why the two open Senate races could take days or weeks is filed below; its expert’s sentence is the honest one: the Mississippi count might take “a very long time—days and weeks.”

Alaska moved by eleven votes and by one point of precincts, and stayed uncalled. The same 8:00 p.m. entry put the Democrat, Mary Peltola, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 votes, against 626 in the evening edition—with the Associated Press Senate file now showing 75.43 percent of precincts reporting, against 74.19 percent at evening. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holds more votes than the margin. Both leaders are below 50 percent, so the ranked-choice tabulation scheduled for November 18 stands ahead of the count, and domestic mail ballots are accepted until November 13 and overseas ballots until November 18, per the accounts filed below.

Kansas’s governorship widened on paper and stayed uncalled in fact.
